title: Confined space entry — fire water tanks, pump wells, pits and risers
activity: Entering a confined space to inspect or service fire protection plant: fire water tank internals, pump wet wells, below-ground valve and booster pits, and sealed riser shafts.

whenRequired:
Any time the work needs a person's head and shoulders to pass the opening of a fire water tank, a pump wet well, a below-ground valve or booster pit, a sealed riser shaft, or any other space that is not built for people to be in. If the job can be done from outside with a pole camera, a mirror or a valve key, no entry permit is opened and the entry steps of this statement do not run. If you are standing at the hatch arguing about whether it counts, it counts.

NO ENTRY DOES NOT MEAN NO DUTIES. Part 4.3 of the Regulation applies to a confined space that could be entered inadvertently by any person (s 62(1)(c)). So whenever the opening is open — entry or not — the space is signed, hard-guarded, and the atmosphere is tested from outside, and the person at the opening stands upwind of anything venting out of it. An open pit lid on a job worked entirely from the surface is the everyday case.

MINIMUM CREW IS THREE for any entry: the entrant, a dedicated standby who does nothing else and never leaves the opening, and a third person for the 000 call, the gate escort and first aid. Two people cannot run the rescue this statement specifies. If the third person is not there, the entry does not start, and that is not tradeable on a two-man run.

Which high risk construction work clauses bite depends on the space in front of you. s 291(a), (f), (l) and (q) apply to essentially every entry on this work, and s 291(k) applies wherever the crew is at a switchboard, a circuit breaker, level electrodes or an alarm circuit — which is almost always. s 291(d) applies where a pre-1990 installation means gaskets, mastics or pipework may be asbestos. s 291(n) and (o) apply where the opening is in a driveway, car park or roadway, or where there is powered mobile plant moving at the opening. Tick the ones that apply on the day on the permit.

The confined space duties in Part 4.3 apply on their own footing whichever way the high risk construction work question falls under Chapter 6. Do not let an argument about s 289 or s 290 be used to skip a permit.
permits: Confined space entry permit — in writing, completed by the nominated competent person and issued by the PCBU before entry (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 67(1) and (2)(a))
Written confined space risk assessment for this specific space, by a competent person (s 66(2) and (3))

Isolation / lock-out-tag-out permit with a written isolation register covering the pumpset, the tank fill line, the suction and outlet valves, the level controls, and any inter-cell balance line, shared overflow or cross-connection to another tank

Electrical isolation signed off by a licensed electrical worker or the site's authorised electrical person — they prove de-energised and do any disconnection; the fire technician's role stops at switching an isolator or breaker off and fitting a padlock and personal danger tag

Fire system impairment notice signed by the building's responsible person, with a maximum impairment duration and a named escalation contact, and a monitoring 'on test' reference number obtained before the first valve is touched
Hot work permit where any cutting, grinding, welding or brazing happens in or at the space (AS 1674.1:2025)
Working at heights permit for roof access, the hatch and the descent where the site or principal contractor requires one
Traffic management plan and a spotter where the opening is in a driveway, car park or roadway
EWP permit and the operator's high risk work licence where an elevating work platform is used to reach the hatch
Principal contractor's permit to work and site induction where the site runs one
Switchboard access authority where the site controls its own switchboards
ppe: Full body harness to AS/NZS 1891.1:2020 Personal equipment for work at height — Manufacturing requirements for full body combination and lower body harnesses, inspected and inside its tag date

Retrieval attachment for vertical extraction — shoulder or sternal retrieval extension straps, a rescue harness or a spreader, so a casualty comes up upright and narrow. The rear D is for fall arrest on the descent only
Restraint line and rated anchor connection for anyone working near a roof edge, on or beside an unrated tank roof, or leaning over an open hatch on a tank holding water
Personal 4-gas monitor (O2, LEL, CO, H2S), bump tested on the day, worn in the breathing zone in continuous alarm mode — it warns, it does not protect
Hard hat with chin strap
Safety glasses; goggles where scale, rust or sludge is being disturbed
Non-slip safety footwear; gumboots where the space holds water
Nitrile or chemical gloves for sludge and coatings; cut-resistant gloves for corroded steelwork
Coveralls, disposable where the space holds bird droppings, sludge or algae
Hearing protection where a pumpset is running nearby, set up so the entrant can still hear the abort signal
ELV IP-rated head torch — no 240V droplights in a wet space
Respiratory protection selected under AS/NZS 1715:2009 for the specific contaminant where coatings, scale or rust are disturbed, or where the work generates vapour or dust

Air supplied respiratory equipment to AS/NZS 1716:2012, used under AS/NZS 1715:2009, where the risk assessment for this space calls for it. Any worker who may don it holds a current fit test for that facepiece (AS/NZS 1715:2009 and AS/NZS ISO 16975.3:2023) and is clean-shaven at the sealing surface. Name the fit-tested crew on the permit. If the space needs an air set and the crew does not have one with fit-tested wearers, the entry does not go ahead

Manually inflated flotation only, where the supervisor has authorised an entry with water that cannot be removed — chosen to work with the harness and confirmed to pass back out through the opening. Never an auto-inflating PFD in a space you have to be winched out of
Hi-vis where there is plant or traffic movement at the opening
training: RIIWHS202E Enter and work in confined spaces — every entrant and the standby person
MSMWHS217 Gas test atmospheres — whoever takes the pre-entry and monitoring readings
PUASAR025 Undertake confined space rescue — the standby, on every entry. On-site no-entry retrieval is always the plan on this work, so the ticket is always required
RIIWHS204E Work safely at heights — roof access, the hatch, the descent and the retrieval rigging
HLTAID011 Provide first aid and HLTAID009 Provide cardiopulmonary resuscitation — at least one current on site
Current respirator fit test for the specific facepiece, for anyone who may wear air supplied respiratory equipment (AS/NZS 1715:2009 and AS/NZS ISO 16975.3:2023)
Licensed electrical worker (or the site's authorised electrical person) attending for any proving de-energised or any disconnection of level electrodes, fill solenoids or alarm circuits
High risk work licence for the class of EWP where an elevating work platform is used to reach the hatch
Competent person nominated in writing to conduct the risk assessment (s 66(2)) and to complete the entry permit (s 67(2)(a))
QBCC fire protection occupational licence for the class of fire protection work being done in the space
CPCWHS1001 Prepare to work safely in the construction industry (white card)
Site induction, and instruction in this SWMS and the emergency procedures before entry (s 76). Records of confined space training are kept for 2 years (s 76(2))

steps.step: Plan the job and check the gear before leaving the yard
hazards: Arriving without the equipment or the people that make entry lawful, and entering anyway to save the trip
Gas detector out of calibration, or a flammable channel that cannot read in the atmosphere this space actually has
Harness, retrieval straps, retrieval line, tripod or winch out of inspection date, or damaged
Crew short of the tickets, or short of the third person the rescue needs
No rescue plan, or one that assumes somebody else will improvise
Entry booked at the end of a long shift, or at an hour when the full rescue arrangement does not hold
Below-ground space entered with a storm in the catchment
Electrical isolations planned to be done by people not licensed to do them

controls.control: Read the last entry record and the AS 1851-2012 log for this space first. If the previous entry found the tank clean and dry and the work can be seen from the hatch, book it as a no-entry job and take the pole camera and the inspection mirror instead of the tripod. The best confined space job is the one nobody enters.

Load the rescue plant the plan actually needs, and do not leave without any of it: tripod or davit with a man-rated retrieval winch, retrieval extension straps or a rescue harness for vertical extraction, spare harness, forced-air blower with enough ducting to reach the BOTTOM of the space, ELV IP-rated lighting, 15m rescue line, sump pump and lead on an RCD, first aid kit and a probe thermometer. This is rescue plant, not personal kit: it is inspected, tagged and maintained on the plant register, because the Regulation requires plant and equipment provided for first aid or emergency rescue to be maintained in good working order (s 74(3)(c)).

Bump test the 4-gas detector with test gas on the day. Calibration must be current against the manufacturer's stated interval, and inside 6 months unless the manufacturer states longer — a bump test does not rescue an overdue calibration. Write the calibration DUE DATE and the bump test result on the permit.

Note the LEL sensor type on the permit. A catalytic-bead flammable sensor has to burn the sample to read it and goes low or zero in a depleted atmosphere. Where this space has any history of oxygen depletion — a closed steel fire tank almost always does — take an instrument with an infrared LEL sensor, which does not need oxygen to read. If the company has not got one on the shelf, say so on the permit and work to the fallback in the atmosphere step: ventilate back to a normal oxygen level and retest before you accept any flammable reading. Then put an infrared instrument on the list to buy — this is the single most common way a tank atmosphere lies to you.

Check the harness, retrieval extension straps, lanyard, retrieval line, tripod and winch carry a current inspection tag, inside the inspection interval required by AS/NZS 1891.4:2025 and the manufacturer's instructions and signed by the person that standard requires for that tier of inspection. Then run them through your hands for cuts, corrosion, heat glazing and distorted hardware. No tag, or a tag out of date, and the gear does not go on the truck.

Confirm the crew is three: entrant, dedicated standby, third person. Every entrant and the standby hold RIIWHS202E, the standby holds PUASAR025, and whoever is gas testing holds MSMWHS217. No ticket, no entry — the job is rescheduled, not covered by supervising someone through it.

Where any isolation involves proving de-energised, or disconnecting level electrodes, a fill solenoid or an alarm circuit, book a licensed electrical worker or the site's authorised electrical person to attend at the isolation and confirm the time. Under the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) s 18(1)(b), testing an electrical installation is electrical work. A fire technician does not do it.

Check the forecast and any severe weather warning before you drive out. No entry into a below-ground valve pit, booster pit or wet well with a severe thunderstorm warning current or heavy rain in the catchment — these spaces fill in minutes.

No confined space entry at the end of a long shift, and no entry outside the hours in which the full arrangement actually holds: three-person crew, fit-tested air set if the space needs one, licensed electrical worker if the isolations need one, and a site contact who answers the phone. Impairments get done early for a reason, but an early start after a late finish is not a plan.

Ring the site contact before you drive out and get the tank or well drawings, the pumpset type (electric or diesel), whether the tank is single or multi-cell or cross-connected to another tank, and who holds the switchboard and pump room keys.

steps.step: On arrival, confirm the space and test whether entry can be avoided
hazards: Treating a space as 'not really confined' because the paperwork is inconvenient
A riser cupboard or booster pit misclassified either way
Unknown previous contents — recent tank coating, treated water, sewer ingress
Asbestos gaskets, mastics or pipework in a pre-1990 installation, disturbed without knowing
Lead-based or coal tar epoxy tank coatings disturbed without knowing
Another trade entering inadvertently while you are set up
Duties dropped because the job was called a no-entry job

controls.control: Try the work from outside first, every time. Tank internals go on a pole camera through the hatch; valve pit valves are usually exercised from the surface with a key and bar; a riser cupboard is worked from the doorway with your body outside the opening. If nobody's head and shoulders pass the opening, it is not an entry — record that on the job and do not open a permit.

Apply the Schedule 19 test to the space in front of you, not to what it is called: enclosed or partly enclosed, not designed or intended primarily to be occupied by a person, at normal atmospheric pressure, and a risk from an atmosphere without a safe oxygen level, from contaminants that may cause injury from fire or explosion, from harmful concentrations of airborne contaminants, or from engulfment. A riser cupboard a person stands in with the door open and free air is usually not a confined space; the same cupboard at the base of a sealed shaft is.

No entry does not switch the duties off. Whenever the opening is open — entry or not — the space is signed under s 68, hard-guarded, and the atmosphere is tested from outside, and the person at the opening stands upwind of anything venting out of it. Heavier-than-air gas coming out of a pit can put down a person who never went in.
Where the classification is arguable, treat it as a confined space and ring the supervisor. Nobody downgrades a space on site to avoid a permit.

Check the site asbestos register before disturbing any gasket, lagging, mastic, coating or pipework in or at the space. On a pre-1990 installation, assume gaskets and mastics may be asbestos-containing until confirmed otherwise. Suspected ACM is a stop work: do not disturb it, report it, and the job is rescheduled under the asbestos SWMS.

Ask what the tank was last coated or lined with, and when, and get the SDS or the coating history before anything gets scraped, ground or cut. Old fire tank linings can be lead-based or coal tar epoxy.

At the end of the job, add the space to the site's confined space register with its internal dimensions, opening size AND shape, depth, access route and rescue arrangement, so the next crew is not making the same call from scratch at 6am. Fill it in from the permit while it is still in your hand, not from memory next week.

steps.step: Impair the fire system and tell the people who need to know, before anything is isolated
hazards: Building left without fire protection and nobody told
Brigade turnout on an unannounced alarm from the work
Monitoring company disconnecting the wrong system
Impairment left open overnight because the job ran long, with nobody escalating
Fire watch agreed verbally and never actually provided

controls.control: Get the building's responsible person to sign the impairment notice before the first valve is touched: which system, which part of it, from when to when, and what protection is left in service.

Agree a MAXIMUM impairment duration in writing on the notice, and name the person to ring the moment the restore time looks like slipping — by name and mobile number, not a job title. If the maximum is reached and the system is not back, the escalation happens whether or not the work is finished.
Ring the monitoring company, place the affected zones on test, and write the reference number on the permit. Get the reference before you isolate, not after the appliances arrive.

Where the impairment leaves a building or a floor with no water — a single tank, a single pumpset — agree a fire watch with the occupier in writing for the duration, name who provides it and what they do, and confirm the person is actually on the floor before the first valve shuts.

Under the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) the occupier keeps their duties for the prescribed fire safety installation while you have it apart. Put the expected restore time in writing and tell them the moment it slips.
Record the impairment in the AS 1851-2012 log book as it starts, not at the end of the day from memory.

steps.step: Isolate, lock and tag every service connected to the space
hazards: Pump auto-starting on a pressure drop with a person in the wet well
Diesel pumpset cranking off its own batteries with the switchboard already isolated
Tank refilling through the ball float valve and engulfing the entrant
The second cell of a twin-cell tank, a shared overflow or a cross-connection reflooding the space with a person in it
Level electrodes calling for a fill as the level drops
Gas suppression discharging into a pump room or riser
Electric shock from a submersible pump, level probes or unrated lighting
Unlicensed person doing electrical work while proving an isolation
Stored energy in pressurised lines released when a flange is cracked

controls.control: Break the connection where you can rather than trusting a valve. Remove a spool piece or fit a blank flange on the fill line. A closed valve is not an isolation; a blank is.

Where the tank is multi-cell or cross-connected to another tank, isolate AND blank the inter-cell balance line, the shared overflow and any cross-connection before entry. Draining one cell while the other stays in service to keep the building protected is how this work is normally done, and a valve between a full cell and the one you are standing in is not an isolation. Walk and record each one on the isolation register with the rest. The same goes for a jockey pump or a town-main bypass that can backfeed into the tank.

Lock the pumpset off at its main isolator with your own padlock and personal danger tag. On a diesel pumpset that is nowhere near enough: isolate both battery banks, close the fuel shut-off, and disable the auto-start pressure switch at the controller. A diesel pump will crank on a pressure drop with the switchboard dead.

Close and lock the tank fill line at the town main isolating valve upstream of the ball float valve. Chain and lock the valve and write its location on the permit. Where there is an automatic fill solenoid, switch its circuit breaker to off and lock it off — switching a breaker off and hanging your own lock and tag on it is not electrical work; going any further is.
Close and lock the tank suction and outlet isolating valves to the pumpset so the space cannot drain suddenly or backfeed while someone is in it.
Where a gas suppression system covers the pump room or riser, put it to isolate at the panel, lock the cylinder actuators off, and record both on the permit.
One lock per person on the group lock box, and the box stays on the isolation. The hardware is the control: while any lock is on, the isolation cannot be restored by anybody.

A licensed electrical worker or the site's authorised electrical person proves de-energised, and carries out any disconnection of level electrodes, fill solenoids or low-level alarm circuits, and signs the isolation register on the permit. The fire technician's electrical role stops at operating an isolator or breaker to the off position and fitting a padlock and personal danger tag. Testing an electrical installation is electrical work under the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) s 18(1)(b), and work on or near energised electrical equipment is governed by the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld), Part 8 Division 3. Do not prove dead yourself, and do not let anyone tell you it is only a test.
Nobody removes another person's lock, for any reason, ever. The last person out of the space takes the last lock off.

Write every isolation point and its location on the permit's isolation register — including the ones the electrical worker proved — and walk them with the standby, so two people have physically seen each one.
Before cracking any flange, assume the line is still pressurised: stand out of the split line, crack it on the far side, and let it bleed before the bolts come out.

steps.responsible: Technician, Supervisor and the licensed electrical worker

steps.step: Get to the hatch — roof access, edges, pit surrounds and traffic
hazards: Walking on a bolted-steel or GRP panel tank roof that was never rated for foot traffic, and falling through it into a full tank
Fall from an unprotected roof edge, or from an external access ladder or an unrated platform
Tripod or davit standing on curved, thin or unrated roof sheeting, or on soft or sloping ground
Vehicle driving over an open pit, over a tripod leg, or over the retrieval line in a driveway or car park
Tools, fittings and hatch bolts dropped from the roof or the access ladder onto people below
Hot steel and hot lid fasteners in the Queensland sun

controls.control: Where the hatch can be reached and the work done without anyone going onto the tank roof — a hatch served by a fixed rated platform, a pit worked from the surface — do it that way and do not go up. Where the roof access itself is the unsafe part, that is a reason not to do the job today, not a reason to be careful.

Reach the hatch on rated access only: a fixed ladder and rated platform, a compliant portable ladder secured top and bottom, or an EWP. Do not walk on a tank roof unless there is a rated walkway or the roof is documented as trafficable. Bolted steel and GRP panel tank roofs are not trafficable, they give way at the panel joint, and the person goes into the water.

Where the opening is in a driveway, car park or roadway, set a hard-barriered exclusion zone sized to cover the tripod footprint AND the full retrieval path, not just the lid. Where the pit is on a road or in an operating car park, a traffic management plan and a spotter, agreed with the site before the lid comes off. A vehicle over a tripod leg is a dropped entrant.

Where the hatch is within 2m of an unprotected edge, or beside roof sheeting not rated for foot traffic, work in RESTRAINT on a rated anchor — a line short enough that you cannot reach the edge or the unrated sheeting at all. Confirm the anchor is rated and documented, and that it is not the tank roof itself, a handrail, a pipe or a vent.

Stand the tripod or davit on ground or structure rated to take the tripod plus a loaded retrieval line: hard, level, clear of the edge of the opening. On a roof that means over a rated structural member or on a purpose-made spreader, never on unsupported sheeting. If you cannot find footing you would trust with a person's weight on the line, the entry does not go ahead.
Physical edge protection or a hard cover over any other opening, vent or skylight on the roof within the work area, before anyone starts moving gear around.

Everything that goes up is tied or bagged, and nothing is carried in a hand on a ladder. Exclusion zone below the access route and below the hatch while gear is going up or coming down, with the third person keeping it clear.
Queensland sun: expect the roof, the lid and the fasteners to be too hot to touch by mid-morning. Do the roof work early, and check the steel with the back of a gloved hand before you grab it.
Hard hat with chin strap, harness on and connected before you go onto the roof or beside the pit, non-slip footwear, gloves, and hi-vis at any opening with plant or traffic movement.

steps.step: Open up, guard, sign and ventilate
hazards: Falling through an open hatch into a full or part-full tank while looking in from the opening — before any entry, and before the retrieval line and the permit controls exist
Someone else stepping into an open hatch or pit
Inadvertent entry by another trade or a curious building occupant
An object dropped down a riser shaft from a level above the entrant
A hatch lid dropping back onto hands
Gas released in the face on cracking the lid
Deep silt or sludge in the sump — engulfment, not mess
Contaminant, or the blower's own exhaust fumes, blown into the space

controls.control: On any tank or well that holds water, the person opening the lid is in a harness on a restraint line from a rated anchor BEFORE the lid moves, and the opening is hard-guarded on every side a person could step or lean in from BEFORE anyone puts their head over it. Hard barrier or a purpose-made hatch guard — not bunting. The guard goes on first and comes off last. Record the depth of water in the tank on the permit.
Never leave an open hatch or pit unattended — not for a minute, not to go back to the ute. If the crew has to leave the opening, the lid goes back on or the opening is hard-covered.

Before entry to a riser shaft, lock or tag every riser access door on every level and notify the building manager in writing. Where a level cannot be secured, hard-barricade that doorway and post the confined space sign at it too. No work in the shaft while any level above the entrant is unsecured. A fitting dropped from level 20 down a riser is not a hard-hat problem.

Ventilate mechanically before and during the entry. Run the blower duct down to the BOTTOM of the space where the heavy gases sit — blowing across the opening does nothing. Purge for at least 20 minutes before the first atmospheric test, and keep the blower running the whole time anyone is inside. The retest result, not the clock, is what authorises entry.
Put the blower intake upwind and clear of vehicle exhausts, generators, site plant and any diesel pumpset exhaust, so you are not pumping carbon monoxide into the space.

Erect the confined space sign at each entry to the space before work starts, and keep it up through setup, the work and pack-up (s 68). It must identify the space and tell workers they must not enter without a confined space entry permit, and it goes clear and prominent right next to the opening.

Never use oxygen or oxygen-enriched air to ventilate or sweeten a space. s 71(1)(b) prohibits purging or ventilating with pure oxygen or mixtures over 21% by volume, and it turns a rusty tank into a bomb.
Stand upwind and to the side when cracking the lid, let the space breathe before your head goes over it, and prop or secure the lid so it cannot fall back onto hands.

Probe the sludge through the opening with a rod and write the sludge depth on the permit before anyone commits to entry. Sludge above knee height is a NO ENTRY until it is removed — that is engulfment. Where engulfment stays a live risk after removal, the engulfment rescue equipment is named on the permit before entry (s 75(3)).
Gloves and eye protection for corroded hatch fasteners — expect scale and rust to come down as it opens.

steps.step: Test the atmosphere from outside, top to bottom
hazards: Oxygen depleted by rust and microbial action in a closed steel fire tank — the classic tank killer, with no smell and no warning
A flammable reading that cannot be trusted because the oxygen is low
Oxygen enrichment from a leaking oxy set or a cylinder left in the pump room
Hydrogen sulphide and methane in stagnant valve pits and wet wells, or from sewer cross-connection
Carbon monoxide drawn in from plant or a diesel pumpset
Solvent vapour from a recent tank lining or coating
A single reading at the hatch missing a layered atmosphere in the sump

controls.control: Test from outside the space with a sampling pump and hose. Nobody puts their head in to take a reading, and nobody 'just has a quick sniff'.

Test at the top, at mid-depth and at the bottom, and along the space where it runs horizontally. Heavy gases lie in the sump, methane sits under the roof. One reading at the hatch tells you nothing about where the entrant is going. Allow the hose its full draw time at each depth before you read.

READ OXYGEN FIRST, and let it tell you whether to believe the rest. A catalytic-bead flammable sensor has to burn the sample to read it, and below roughly 10% oxygen it reads low or zero whatever is in there. Never accept 0% LEL in a depleted atmosphere: ventilate back to a normal oxygen level and retest before you believe the flammable channel at all. '0% LEL, 15% oxygen' is one real number and one meaningless one.

Entry is authorised only on oxygen between 19.5% and 23.5% by volume, flammable gas or vapour below 5% of its LEL, and every contaminant below its workplace exposure standard. Those are the Regulation's numbers — Schedule 19 safe oxygen level, and s 72 — not house rules. Write each reading, its depth and the time on the permit.

Below 19.5% oxygen, or a contaminant over its exposure standard: ventilate and retest. The Regulation's primary duty is that the atmosphere of the space HAS a safe oxygen level (s 71(2)(a)); air supplied respiratory equipment is a fallback under s 71(2)(b) only where a safe oxygen level is not reasonably practicable. It is a separate written decision by the supervisor, on gear to AS/NZS 1716:2012 used under AS/NZS 1715:2009, worn by a fit-tested clean-shaven worker, with a rescue plan that assumes the atmosphere will kill an unprotected rescuer. Do not reach for a respirator as a shortcut around ventilating.

Above 23.5% oxygen there is no entry and no respirator workaround — s 71(2) offers no fallback for enrichment, and this is an ignition problem, not a breathing one. Find and stop the source: a leaking oxy-acetylene set, an oxygen cylinder left in the pump room or riser. Remove it, ventilate with air only, and retest. Oxygen enrichment turns a rusty tank into a bomb.
Between 5% and 10% of LEL, everybody out unless a suitably calibrated continuous-monitoring flammable gas detector is used in the space. At 10% of LEL or above, out, no discussion (s 72(2)).
Retest before every re-entry, after any break, and after any change — the blower stopping, a valve moving, hot work starting, a smell that was not there before.

Every entrant wears a personal 4-gas monitor in the breathing zone in continuous alarm mode for the whole entry. Be clear about what it is: the pre-entry test from outside is what authorises the entry, and the personal monitor is a warning device. It protects nobody on its own — it buys the seconds in which the entrant gets out.

steps.step: Issue the entry permit and set the crew, standby, retrieval and comms
hazards: An opening too small or too obstructed to get a casualty out through
Entry with no permit, or on a permit copied from the last job
Two-person crew that cannot run its own rescue
Standby person given other work, or wandering off to hold a torch
Standby who has never operated the winch under load
Two entrants inside with one retrieval system
Casualty winched on a rear D, folded forward and jammed in the hatch
No way for the entrant to raise the alarm
Rescue left to improvisation, or handed to an emergency service that never agreed to it

controls.control: HOLD POINT — measure the opening. Write its dimensions and shape on the permit. Confirm with the gear in your hands that the retrieval device and a casualty in a harness with retrieval straps will physically pass through it, and that nothing obstructs it: pipework, the ladder head, the davit foot, the blower duct, a bolted-down grate. The Regulation requires the entry and exit openings to be large enough to allow emergency access and to be unobstructed (s 74(3)(a) and (b)). If a casualty cannot be extracted through this opening, the entry does not go ahead — and that is a defect to report on the building, not a problem to work around.

Rig the tripod or davit over the opening with a man-rated retrieval winch, and connect the retrieval line before the entrant's feet leave the ground. Connect it to shoulder or sternal retrieval extension straps, a rescue harness or a spreader, so an unconscious person comes up UPRIGHT AND NARROW. The rear D is a fall-arrest attachment for the descent: winching a limp person on a rear D folds them forward at the waist and jams them across a 450mm hatch, which is how a retrieval becomes a recovery.

Continuous communication from outside the space for the whole entry (s 69): voice where the space allows it, hard-wired comms or an agreed rope-tug code where a steel tank kills radio. Prove the comms work before the entrant is out of sight, and say the abort signal out loud so everyone has heard it.

HOLD POINT — minimum crew of three: the entrant, a dedicated standby who does nothing else and never leaves the opening, and a third person for the 000 call, the gate escort and first aid. If the third person is not there, the entry does not start. The rescue in this statement is three jobs at once, and one person cannot do it.

One entrant in the space at a time. A second entrant only where a SECOND independent retrieval system is rigged and a SECOND standby is present, both recorded on the permit. One winch retrieves one person.

The nominated competent person completes the written entry permit and the business issues it before anyone enters (s 67(1) and (2)(a)): the space it relates to, the names of the persons permitted to enter, the period of time during which the work will be carried out, and the measures to control risk, based on the written risk assessment and including the s 69 system of work. It carries space for the acknowledgement that the work is complete and all persons have left.

The standby stays at the opening for the whole entry, does nothing else, and never enters. Their job is the s 69 system of work: continuous communication with the entrant, and monitoring conditions inside the space. Counting stock, answering the phone or helping at the switchboard are not compatible with being the standby. Be honest about what this is — a person watching is not an isolation, it is the reason somebody notices in time.

Before the FIRST entry of the day the standby demonstrates a retrieval on the rigged winch: line loaded, handle and brake proven, casualty path clear, hands knowing where they go. The abort signal is agreed out loud. A full documented rescue drill for this class of space is run at least every 12 months, and the date of the last drill is written on the permit. s 74(1)(b) requires the rescue procedures to be practised as necessary to make them efficient and effective — reading them is not practising them.

The rescue plan for every entry is on-site no-entry retrieval by the standby on the rigged winch, written on the permit. Queensland Fire and Rescue are the backup and are notified — they are never the plan, and no fire and rescue service gives an advance guarantee of a response time to hang an entry on. If on-site retrieval cannot be rigged for this space, the entry does not go ahead.
Full body harness to AS/NZS 1891.1:2020 with the retrieval attachment fitted, worn and buddy-checked at the hatch — not carried down and put on at the bottom.

steps.responsible: Supervisor as competent person, and Standby person

steps.step: Entry and descent
hazards: Fall down the shaft or through the hatch
Corroded internal ladder failing under load — fire tank ladders sit in wet chlorinated air for decades and go at the fixings
Slipping on wet or algae-coated steel
Tools dropped onto the entrant below
Head strike on internals, tie rods and roof supports
Entrant fainting on the ladder in a depleted atmosphere

controls.control: Where the descent is more than a couple of rungs, do not use the tank's own internal ladder at all. Descend on the winch, or on a ladder you brought and secured. The fall is still there — you are swapping unknown corroded steel for gear you can see the tag on.

Fall arrest for the descent: retrieval line under tension on the winch, or a self-retracting device rated for the fall distance and for rescue, anchored to the tripod or to a rated anchor. Free-climbing an open shaft is not on, at any depth.

If the internal ladder is used at all, load it from outside first with a rope pull and inspect the top fixings and the stiles for rust-through before anyone weights it. In doubt, do not use it — and raise it as a defect on the job.
Descend feet first, three points of contact, hands empty. Tools go down in a bag on a separate line once the entrant is at the bottom and clear — never in a hand, a pocket or a belt.
One person on the ladder or line at a time. The standby confirms the entrant is at the bottom and the retrieval line is tended before anyone else moves.
The entrant calls the bottom on the comms, reads out their personal monitor, and confirms the abort signal. The standby writes the entry time on the permit.
Hard hat with chin strap, non-slip footwear, gloves, personal gas monitor clipped in the breathing zone.

steps.step: Do the work inside the space
hazards: Heat stress in a steel tank in a Queensland summer — internals well over 40 degrees with no air movement
Residual water and sludge in the sump: drowning and slipping
Rising water in a below-ground pit or wet well during a storm
Biological contamination — bird droppings, algae, legionella in warm stagnant water, leptospirosis in pits
Rust, scale and old coatings raising dust when disturbed — old fire tank linings can be lead-based or coal tar epoxy
Airborne contaminant generated by the work itself — solvent-based lining or re-coating, abrasive descaling, cutting
Electric shock from unrated lighting or 240V tools in a wet space
Hot work igniting a flammable atmosphere, a tank liner or accumulated sludge
Entrant becoming unwell out of the standby's sight
Noise from a pumpset running on the other side of the wall

controls.control: Do not take hot work into the space if there is any other way to do the job — bolt, clamp or mechanically join rather than weld inside a tank. Where it is unavoidable it is a separate hot work permit: retest the atmosphere immediately before and monitor continuously during, remove or wet down combustibles, fire watch inside and out, and a post-work fire watch of at least 60 minutes after the last spark. Treat that 60 minutes as the Safe QLD house rule — do not quote it as a figure from AS 1674.1:2025. Where the standard, the site permit or the insurer requires longer, the longer time wins.

Battery tools instead of 240V leads into a wet space. Where mains is unavoidable, feed it through an RCD at the source and use ELV IP-rated lighting. A 240V droplight in a wet steel tank is how people die in here.
Pump the sump down below drowning depth before entry and keep the pump running for the whole entry, powered from outside on an RCD.

The blower runs the entire entry, ducted to the bottom of the space. Where the work itself generates airborne contaminant — coating, lining, descaling, cutting — put the ventilation rate up and monitor the atmosphere CONTINUOUSLY rather than spot testing, because the atmosphere you tested is not the atmosphere you are making.

HOLD POINT on water. If the sump cannot be pumped below drowning depth, the entry does not proceed on a life jacket. It proceeds only on a written supervisor decision recorded on the permit, with the retrieval line under tension for the whole entry, and any flotation manually inflated only, chosen to work with the harness, and confirmed to pass back out through the opening. An auto-inflating PFD fires in the water and wedges the casualty in the hatch you have to winch them through, and no flotation at all helps a person face-down in 300mm of sludge.

ABORT TRIGGERS, and they are not negotiable: the personal monitor alarms; the blower stops; comms lost and not restored within 30 seconds; water rising in the space; a smell that was not there before; the entrant sounds wrong. The entrant leaves FIRST and asks the question from outside. No exceptions, no finishing the last bracket.

Queensland heat. Lower the probe thermometer through the hatch and write the temperature inside the space on the permit before entry, and again at each rotation. Under 30 degrees inside: 30 minute rotations. Over 35 degrees inside: 15 minute rotations. At 40 degrees inside the entry stops until the space is cooled or the work moves to the cool of the morning. Iced water, wet towels and a shaded seat with air movement staged AT THE HATCH, not a warm bottle in the ute. A worker who is new, back from leave or not acclimatised gets half the rotation for their first week. The standby watches for slurred speech, confusion, stumbling and a person who has stopped sweating. Nobody 'just finishes it' at 45 degrees inside.
The standby keeps the entrant in sight where the space allows it and in continuous voice contact where it does not, and logs a check every few minutes on the permit.

Before disturbing coatings, scale or rust, stop and confirm what the coating is: SDS or coating history on site, and the asbestos register checked for gaskets, mastics and pipework on a pre-1990 installation. If you cannot find out what it is, do not grind it — treat the coating as a separate hazardous chemicals assessment and come back.

Respiratory protection selected under AS/NZS 1715:2009 for the specific contaminant wherever coatings, scale or rust are disturbed or the work generates vapour or dust. Tight-fitting facepieces only on a fit-tested, clean-shaven worker. Coveralls and safety glasses do nothing about what you are breathing.

Coveralls, nitrile gloves and eye protection where there is sludge, bird droppings or algae. Wash hands and face before eating, and report any flu-like illness in the following fortnight to the supervisor, naming the pit.
Hearing protection where a pumpset is running nearby, set up so the entrant can still hear the abort signal.

steps.step: Exit, account for everyone, close the permit
hazards: A person left inside when the lid goes on
Tools, rags or lighting left in the building's fire water supply
Permit left open and the space still signed as live
Hatch or pit left open after the crew moves on
Records not kept, so nothing can be reconstructed after an incident

controls.control: Close and secure the hatch or lid, and only then remove the guard and the signage. The opening is never left open behind the crew.

The standby does a headcount against the names on the permit before the hatch is touched, and says the count out loud. Then a torch over the whole space, corner to corner, to SEE it empty. The acknowledgement that the work is complete and all persons have left is completed by the competent person (s 67(4)), not by whoever is closest to the clipboard.
Tool count out matches tool count in, written down before entry. A spanner left in a fire tank finds a pump impeller on the day the building needs it.
Retrieve the blower duct, lighting, leads, rags and packaging. This tank is the building's water supply — nothing stays in it.

Records. Keep the confined space entry permit at least until the work it relates to is completed, and the risk assessment for at least 28 days after the work it relates to is completed (s 77(2)). Keep this SWMS until the high risk construction work is completed (s 303(1)), readily accessible to the crew and available for inspection. Where a notifiable incident occurred in connection with the work, keep the permit, the risk assessment and the SWMS for at least 2 years after the incident (s 77(3) and s 303(2)) — and leave the site alone.

steps.step: De-isolate, return the fire system to service and hand back
hazards: System left impaired with the crew gone and the paperwork closed
Tank refilled with the suction valve still shut
Fire pump started dry or against a closed suction
Air-locked suction line and a pump that will not prime when called
Crew leaving before a large tank has refilled to design low-water level
A critical defect found inside the space and never notified to the occupier
Monitoring left on test, or the panel left with isolations in
Occupier never told the building is protected again

controls.control: Open the suction and outlet valve before the fill valve, confirm it is fully open, and strap or lock it in the open position. A pumpset run against a shut suction destroys itself in seconds.
Refill the tank and watch the fill. A ball float valve that sticks is a defect found now or a flood found later.

Restore the pumpset properly: batteries on, fuel valve open, auto-start pressure switch back in service, controller to AUTO, then prove it with a test start and confirm it primes, runs and stops as the AS 1851-2012 routine requires. A fire pump is never left in manual.

HOLD POINT — the system is not handed back and the impairment is not closed until the tank level is confirmed at or above the design low-water level AND the pumpset has proven in AUTO on a test start. A big tank takes hours to refill, so decide before you start who is staying with it. If nobody can stay, the impairment stays OPEN, the fire watch stays on, the monitoring stays on test, the occupier is told in writing that the system is still down, and a named person comes back to close it out. A closed impairment on a half-full tank is a lie on paper and it is signed with your name.

Remove locks in reverse order, each person taking their own, and only after the standby confirms the space is clear and closed. The licensed electrical worker restores anything they isolated, proved or disconnected, and signs it off on the isolation register.

CRITICAL DEFECT NOTICE. Where anything found inside the space is a critical defect under the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 49 — a defect likely to render the installation inoperable, and reasonably likely to have a significant adverse impact on the safety of occupants if a fire happens — give the occupier a critical defect notice in the approved form WITHIN 24 HOURS after you carry out the maintenance (s 53), and keep a copy on the job. That duty is on the person who did the work, not on the building. A pump defect that makes the hydrants inoperable is the Regulation's own example. The maintenance itself must be carried out in compliance with QDC part MP6.1 (s 50).
Take the monitoring off test against the same reference number, confirm the panel is normal with no faults or isolations remaining, and have the monitoring company confirm signals are being received.

Close the impairment with the building's responsible person in writing with the time, stand the fire watch down, and record the entry, the defects found inside the space and the return to service in the AS 1851-2012 log book.

steps.responsible: Technician, Supervisor and the licensed electrical worker

steps.step: Monitor the controls on the job, and review this statement
hazards: Controls written down here but not actually in place on the day
Work drifting away from this statement mid-job and nobody stopping it
A near miss absorbed on the job and never fed back
This statement going stale as the space, the plant, the standards or the law change
Crew signing a statement they have never been taken through

controls.control: VERIFICATION AT ISSUE. The competent person physically checks the controls item by item against the permit before signing it: isolations walked with the standby, electrical isolation signed by the licensed electrical worker, opening measured, gas readings written with depths and times, retrieval rigged and demonstrated, crew of three present, comms proven, abort signal said out loud, water and sludge depths recorded. Signing the permit IS the verification — it is not a formality on the way to starting.

MONITORING DURING THE WORK. The standby monitors the controls continuously for the whole entry — atmosphere, blower, comms, retrieval line, the entrant — and stops the work the moment one of them fails. Where the work is not being carried out in accordance with this statement, it stops immediately or as soon as it is safe to do so, and resumes only in accordance with it (s 300).

SPOT CHECK. The supervisor attends at least one entry per crew per quarter, unannounced, checks it against this statement, and writes down what they found — including what was being done differently and why. A control nobody can actually carry out at 6am gets changed here, not argued about after an incident.

REVIEW TRIGGERS. This statement is reviewed and revised after any incident or near miss on this work; on any change to the space, the plant, the crew arrangement or the method; on a change to the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) or the Confined spaces Code of Practice; on a new edition or amendment of any standard it cites; and in any case at least every 12 months. Where control measures are revised, this statement must be reviewed and as necessary revised (s 302), and the risk assessment for the space is reviewed and revised by a competent person to match (s 66(5)).

INSTRUCTION AND ACCESS. Every entrant, standby and supervisor is taken through this statement and the emergency procedures before entry and signs it (s 76). The training record is kept for 2 years (s 76(2)). A copy of this statement stays on the job, readily accessible to the crew and available for inspection (s 303(3) and (4)), and it is written to be understood by the people using it — if a control on it cannot be read and followed at the hatch, it is the wrong control.

steps.responsible: Supervisor, with the competent person and the Standby person

emergency:
NO-ENTRY RESCUE FIRST, EVERY TIME.

On any alarm — the gas monitor going off, no answer on comms, the entrant going quiet or slurring, the abort signal, water rising in the space — the standby DOES NOT ENTER. They keep the blower running, wind the entrant out on the retrieval line that is already attached, and call the emergency. That is why the crew is three: the standby stays on the winch, the third person makes the 000 call and goes to the street.

Call 000. Say "confined space, person down" and name the space: fire tank, pump well, valve pit, riser shaft. Give the site address the way an ambulance needs it, name the nearest gate or access point, and send the third person to the street to meet them and walk them in. Queensland Fire and Rescue (QFR) are notified as the backup — they are never the plan, and the retrieval does not wait for them.

DO NOT SEND A SECOND PERSON IN AFTER THE FIRST. The second entrant is the one who usually dies. Safe QLD house rule, and it is deliberately stricter than the Regulation: nobody enters a confined space for rescue on this work without air supplied respiratory equipment they are fit-tested for, their own standby outside, and the same controls that applied to the original entry. (The Regulation's own duty, s 75(2), requires air supplied respiratory equipment for a rescuer where the atmosphere does not have a safe oxygen level, has a harmful concentration of an airborne contaminant, or there is a serious risk of it becoming either while the rescuer is in the space. On this work you will not know which of those is true in time, so we treat it as always. Where an engulfment has occurred or is a serious risk, suitable PPE for that must also be available to the rescuer — s 75(3).)

Once the casualty is out and clear of the opening: airway, breathing, CPR by the first aider, oxygen where trained and it is available. Move them into moving air and out of the sun — not into the shade of the tank, which is radiating heat. Tell the paramedics what the monitor was reading and hand them the instrument.

Ring the supervisor immediately, then the office.

WHAT HAS TO BE NOTIFIED. A notifiable incident under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) s 35 is a death (s 36 covers the meaning of serious injury or illness — including medical treatment within 48 hours of exposure to a substance), a serious injury or illness, OR a dangerous incident. A DANGEROUS INCIDENT IS NOTIFIABLE EVEN WHERE NOBODY IS HURT (s 37): an uncontrolled escape of gas from the space, an uncontrolled escape or leakage of a substance, a fire or explosion, an electric shock, a fall or release of plant from a height, an isolation that failed, an entrant who had to be retrieved and walked away fine. On this work the uninjured near miss is the common one and it is the one crews swallow. If in doubt, ring it in. Workplace Health and Safety Queensland is notified immediately on 1300 362 128 (s 38), and the site is not disturbed beyond making it safe and helping the injured until an inspector says otherwise (s 39). Leave the permit, the risk assessment, the isolations and the gas monitor exactly as they are.

IF THE EMERGENCY IS FIRE, FLOODING, RISING WATER OR AN UNCONTROLLED DISCHARGE rather than a person down: everyone out, close the opening if it is safe to do so, evacuate to the assembly point and account for the crew. Then remember the building's fire system is probably still impaired — get to the fire panel, restore what can be safely restored, and tell the brigade on arrival exactly which systems are off and which valves are shut. Hand them the impairment notice.

What are the dimensions AND shape of the opening, and will a casualty in a harness on retrieval straps pass through it? Anything obstructing it — pipework, ladder head, grate, davit foot?
How is the hatch reached — fixed ladder and rated platform, portable ladder, or EWP? Is the tank roof rated for foot traffic, and where is the rated anchor?
Where can the tripod or davit stand so the retrieval line is directly over the opening, and is that ground or structure rated to take the tripod plus a loaded line?
Is the opening in a driveway, car park or roadway? What vehicle or powered mobile plant movement is there at the opening, and who provides the traffic management plan and spotter?
Where is the pumpset main isolator, and who holds the key to the switchboard or pump room?
Is the fire pumpset electric or diesel? If diesel, where are the battery isolators, the fuel shut-off and the auto-start pressure switch?
Where is the tank fill isolating valve on the town main, and is there an automatic fill solenoid? Where is its circuit breaker?
Where is the tank suction and outlet isolating valve to the pumpset?
Is the tank single or multi-cell, is it cross-connected to another tank, and where are the balance line, shared overflow and interconnect valves?
Who is the licensed electrical worker (or the site's authorised electrical person) attending to prove the isolations and disconnect the level electrodes, and what time are they booked for?
How much residual water and sludge is in the space, how deep is the sludge, and how will it be removed before entry?
Is there a gas suppression system covering the pump room or riser? Where is its panel and where are the cylinder actuators?
If this is a riser shaft: how many levels does it serve, who can secure the riser access doors on every level, and how will that be confirmed in writing?

Was this installation built before 1990, and does the site asbestos register cover the gaskets, mastics and pipework at this space? What is the tank coating or lining, and is the SDS or coating history available?
Who is today's crew of three — entrant, dedicated standby, third person — and what are the standby's RIIWHS202E and PUASAR025 ticket numbers?
When was the last documented confined space rescue drill for this class of space, and who ran it?
Who on the crew is fit-tested for the air set, for which facepiece, and when does the fit test expire?
Is there mobile coverage at the opening and inside the space? If not, what comms will be used and what is the agreed abort signal?
What is the forecast, and is there any severe weather warning or heavy rain in the catchment for a below-ground space today?
What temperature is it inside the space, and what time of day is the work being done?
What is the site address and nearest gate as an ambulance would need it, and where is the emergency assembly point?
Who is the building's responsible person for the impairment, what is the maximum impairment duration agreed, and who is the named escalation contact if the restore time slips?
Is the system monitored, by which monitoring company, and what is the account and on-test reference number?
Who provides the fire watch while the system is impaired, and are they on the floor before the first valve shuts?
How long will the tank take to refill to the design low-water level, and does the crew have the hours to stay until it is there?

title: Electrical Work — Fire System Wiring, Panels, Batteries and Mains Supply
activity: Electrical work on fire detection and suppression systems: isolating and proving dead, working inside fire indicator panels with 240 V present, energised testing where it genuinely cannot be avoided, replacing battery banks, running and terminating cable to the Wiring Rules, and work on the submain feeding a fire pump.

hrcw.clause: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(k)
hrcw.text: is carried out on or near energised electrical installations or services

whenRequired:
WHEN YOU NEED THIS SWMS. Any time you will have the cover off something carrying 240 V or more — a fire indicator panel, an ASE, an EWIS or occupant warning rack, a switchboard, a fire pump controller — or you are cutting, replacing or terminating cable, or changing out a battery bank. You do not need it to press TEST at the panel front, walk a building with a smoke tester, or read battery volts off the display.

IS IT CONSTRUCTION WORK? START FROM YES. Maintenance and testing of a fire system is construction work: Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 289(2)(e) captures 'the installation, testing or maintenance of an essential service in relation to a structure', and a fire detection and alarm system is an essential service. Work only falls out of Chapter 6 if it is genuinely 'testing, maintenance or repair work of a minor nature carried out in connection with a structure' (s 289(3)(d)) — and that is a call made job by job, not a blanket exemption for routine AS 1851 service. If you have the cover off, assume it is construction work and this SWMS applies. And note there is no no-paperwork path either way: Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 199 independently requires a recorded risk assessment and a safe work method statement before ANY electrical work on or near energised electrical equipment, whether or not the job is construction work.

WHAT 'NEAR' MEANS. 'Near' is not a matter of judgement. Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 193 defines it: near, in relation to electrical equipment, means within 3 m of an exposed energised part of the equipment. Once the FIP door is open with the mains terminal block, transformer or charger exposed, everyone standing inside that 3 m is in energised electrical work and Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) ss 199-204 apply to them — not just to the person with hands in the panel. That includes a second technician, an apprentice, and the building manager who came to watch.

WHAT THIS SWMS DOES NOT COVER. The high risk construction work this statement covers is Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 291(k) — work carried out on or near energised electrical installations or services. If the same job also involves any of the following, each is a separate high risk construction work category in its own right: a risk of falling more than 2 m (s 291(a)); disturbance of asbestos (s 291(d)); work in or near a confined space such as a pump room pit, tank or valve pit (s 291(f)); or work in an area that may have a contaminated or flammable atmosphere, including a vented (flooded) cell battery room (s 291(l)). Hot work is covered by its own permit and SWMS. Add the matching SWMS. Do not stretch this one over them.

WHO IS A SAFETY OBSERVER. Safety observer means a person who meets the definition in Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) schedule 10 — competent to implement control measures in an emergency or to avoid an emergency, competent to rescue and resuscitate a worker carrying out the work if necessary, and assessed in the previous 12 months as competent to rescue and resuscitate a person. The observer observes the work and does nothing else. A second pair of hands is not a safety observer. An apprentice is not a safety observer. A fire technician without an electrical background is not a safety observer. An observer is not required only where the work consists only of testing AND the recorded s 199(1)(a) risk assessment shows there is no serious risk associated with the proposed work (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 203(3)).

WHO IS AUTHORISED. Energised electrical work is performed only by workers named on Safe QLD's current list of workers authorised to perform energised electrical work, held with this SWMS on the job cover sheet. The technician does not self-certify. Authorisation for a particular job is given by the Safe QLD supervisor after consulting the person with management or control of the workplace — the building manager or occupier (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 199(1)(e)).

HOW RISK IS RATED IN THIS DOCUMENT (the Safe QLD 5 x 5 matrix). CONSEQUENCE: Catastrophic — fatality or permanent disability (electrocution, arc blast, fall from height, an unprotected building that burns). Major — serious injury needing hospital admission (arc flash burns, a shock with cardiac effects). Moderate — injury needing medical treatment and lost time (a burn, a crush, a strain). Minor — first aid only. Insignificant — no injury. LIKELIHOOD: Almost certain — expected on most jobs of this type. Likely — will probably occur at some point. Possible — could occur. Unlikely — could occur but not expected. Rare — only in exceptional circumstances. BANDS: EXTREME — catastrophic or major consequence at possible likelihood or higher; work does not start without the full control set applied and verified. HIGH — catastrophic or major consequence at unlikely likelihood, or moderate at likely or higher; supervisor authorisation required, work does not proceed on the technician's own authority. MEDIUM — moderate consequence at possible or lower, or minor at likely or higher; proceed with the controls applied and the step monitored. LOW — minor or insignificant consequence at unlikely or lower; proceed. Every initialRisk in this document is the rating BEFORE the controls in that step; every residualRisk is the rating with all of those controls actually applied — not with them merely written down.

HOW THE CONTROLS ARE IMPLEMENTED, MONITORED AND REVIEWED (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 299(2)(d) and Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 200(d)). IMPLEMENTED: by the person named in 'responsible' for each step, in the order the steps are written, with the site-specific questions answered on site before the first cover comes off. MONITORED: (1) before work starts, the lead technician confirms on the job card that every worker has signed on to this SWMS and that the site matches the plan; (2) the isolation is independently confirmed by a second worker, who initials the job card, before any cover comes off; (3) during energised work the safety observer confirms — and keeps confirming — that barriers are in place, that the isolation point is clear and reachable, that tools and instruments are in test date, and that nobody unauthorised has come inside the barrier; (4) fire-stopping, cable support and segregation are checked and photographed by a second person before anything is covered; (5) at handback the lead technician verifies against this statement that every isolation made has been removed, every disturbed device tested, and the pumpset proved running. REVIEWED: this SWMS is reviewed and, as necessary, revised whenever the relevant control measures are revised under Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 38 (s 302), and in any case on the first of — a notifiable incident, a serious electrical incident, a dangerous electrical event or a near miss on this work; a change of panel platform, switchboard or site conditions; a change in the law or in a standard this statement relies on; a worker raising a concern about any control in it; or twelve months from the date it was prepared. A revised statement is re-signed by every worker before work resumes under it.

STOP WORK. If any control in this SWMS cannot be applied as written, the work stops immediately, or as soon as it is safe to do so, and resumes only in accordance with this statement (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 300(2)). A residual risk of HIGH is not a licence to proceed — it means the work does not go ahead on the technician's own authority. It goes back to the supervisor, and if the residual cannot be brought below high, the work is not done energised. Any worker on this job may stop it, at any time, for any safety reason, without consequence of any kind.

VERSION, SIGN-ON AND RETENTION. The job cover sheet carried with this statement records: version number and date prepared; who prepared it; the workers consulted in preparing it; the list of workers authorised to perform energised electrical work; and the worker sign-on table (name, licence number, signature, date) which every worker on the job completes before starting and completes again if this statement is revised. Where the work is high risk construction work in connection with a construction project, a copy goes to the principal contractor before the work commences (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 301). RETENTION: keep this SWMS until the work it relates to is complete, and for at least 2 years after a notifiable incident occurring in connection with that work (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 303). For energised electrical work, keep the recorded risk assessment for at least 28 days after the work is completed and this SWMS until the work is completed, and keep both for at least 2 years if a serious electrical incident or dangerous electrical event occurs in connection with the work (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 204). A copy stays readily accessible to every worker on the job and available for inspection.

Electrical isolation permit with personal lock and danger tag (lock-out tag-out), one lock per worker. The tag is a warning sign attached to the isolating device in a prominent position and suitable in the circumstances, having regard to AS 1319 (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 198(2)(a))

Energised electrical work authorisation — recorded before the work starts, naming which exception in Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 195(1) is relied on and why; supported by the recorded risk assessment required by s 199(1)(a) and a SWMS complying with s 200; authorised by the Safe QLD supervisor after consulting the person with management or control of the workplace (s 199(1)(e))
Site contractor access / permit to work from the building manager, including after-hours access to plant rooms and risers
Fire pump impairment notice to the occupier where the pumpset submain is being isolated

Site asbestos register and asbestos management plan sighted before any drilling, cutting or fixing into an existing wall, floor, ceiling or panel backing board. No register is a stop. Electrically retested at the interval Safe QLD's PPE schedule requires and within the retest date marked on the glove; visually inspected and roll (air) tested by the wearer immediately before every use. A glove with no legible date does not go on
Arc-rated face shield plus arc-rated balaclava at switchboards, fire pump controllers and battery terminals
Clear safety glasses to AS/NZS 1337.1 worn under the face shield and at all times in the plant room
Safety footwear to AS/NZS 2210.3 of a non-conductive / electrically insulating classification. Footwear is a backstop, never a primary shock control — it does not make it safe to touch anything
Nitrile chemical gloves and face shield when handling batteries; eyewash or clean running water confirmed within reach before the first terminal nut is loosened
Hearing protection in the pump room whenever the pumpset may run
Hard hat where there is fixed plant, pipework or a riser overhead
Rated, in-date, dry insulating mat to stand on at any panel or board being worked on with parts energised
Insulated 1000 V hand tools to AS IEC 60900 (tools are not PPE, but they are non-negotiable on this job, and they are in test date and inspected before use)
