whenRequired:
Fill this in before any job where you will make a spark, a flame or a hot surface on site — grinder, cut-off saw, oxy set, welder, or a soldering/brazing torch. That includes a two minute cut on a bracket. Fill it in again if the location, the plant or the fire system isolation changes during the day.

Not every high risk construction work classification above applies to every job. (a) applies when any of the work is above 2 m. (d) applies when you will cut or drill into building fabric that may contain asbestos. (j) applies when you are working on or near chemical, fuel or refrigerant lines. (k), (l) and (o) apply on nearly every plant room job. Tick the ones that are in scope for the day on the front of this SWMS before anyone signs it.

The hot work permit runs to a maximum of 8 hours (AS 1674.1). If the work stops for more than 2 hours, or runs past the finish time written on the permit, the permit is finished — get a new one before the next spark. Do not let a long day quietly run on an expired permit.

It does not cover hot work inside a tank, pit, riser or pump well — that is confined space work and needs its own SWMS and an entry permit.
permits: Hot work permit, signed by the building's responsible person before any spark. It is not a Queensland statutory permit — it is required by AS 1674.1, the site and the building's insurer — but no permit means no hot work. Maximum currency 8 hours. A new permit is required if the work stops for more than 2 hours or runs past the finish time on the permit.
Fire system impairment / isolation permit signed by the occupier or building manager, with the isolation entered on the site isolation register and a time it must be back on.

ASE isolate booked with the QFD monitoring contractor (Johnson Controls, 1300 360 575) before isolating. Write the isolation reference they give you on the permit. Before you isolate, confirm with the building's responsible person that the occupier's own alternative protection arrangement for the isolation period is in place — QFD requires protection at least equivalent to the monitored system while the alarm is isolated, and this SWMS's interim measures are what deliver it. An isolate longer than 12 hours needs Queensland Fire Department approval.
Site permit to work or contractor induction where the building runs its own system — hospital, aged care, club, cold store, data centre, shopping centre.
Working at heights permit where the site requires one for EWP, scaffold or roof access.
Confined space entry permit if any part of the hot work is inside a tank, pit, riser or pump well. That work is outside this SWMS and needs its own, written to AS 2865.
Electrical isolation permit or lock-out tag-out where a pump controller, FIP supply or switchboard has to be de-energised — licensed electrical worker only.
ppe: Cotton drill long sleeve shirt and trousers, sleeves down and buttoned, no synthetics, no frayed or oily clothing
Welding helmet with the correct shade filter to AS/NZS 1338.1 (low shade for oxy and brazing, dark shade for arc), safety glasses worn underneath
Face shield over safety glasses to AS/NZS 1337.1 for grinding and disc cutting

P2 half-face respirator, fit-tested, selected and used to AS/NZS 1715 and AS/NZS 1716 — P3 or powered air for galvanised pipe, stainless, or a plant room with no ventilation. A P2 or P3 filter stops particulate only. It does nothing for the ozone, nitrogen dioxide or carbon monoxide that come off an arc, and nothing for fluoride flux fume — those need extraction or forced ventilation, and a respirator is not a substitute for either. In a small unventilated room with no extraction available, the work does not proceed.
Class 5 earmuffs or plugs to AS/NZS 1270 for grinding and cut-off work
Leather welding gloves for hot work; cut-resistant gloves for handling cut pipe and swarf. No oil or grease on gloves that will touch oxygen fittings.
Leather apron and spats where sparks fall onto the body or into boots
Lace-up safety boots to AS/NZS 2210.3
Full body harness and lanyard to AS/NZS 1891, anchored to the manufacturer's anchor point, when working from a boom-type EWP
Hard hat to AS/NZS 1801 and hi-vis to AS/NZS 4602.1 where the site or overhead work requires it
training: QBCC fire protection occupational licence covering the system in front of you. The classes are streamed — there are separate install-and-maintain classes and separate certify classes, and a certify class is not implied by an install-and-maintain class. Read the class printed on your own card and match it to the system you are about to work on. If your card does not cover it, you do not touch it.

Welding on sprinkler or hydrant pressure pipework — welder qualified for the welding procedure to the standard the installation was built to. Check that before you strike an arc on a pressure line, not after.
General construction induction card — white card, CPCWHS1001 — WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 316 and 317
Hot work permit receiver training, and a documented fire watch briefing for whoever holds the watch
Welding competency for the process being used (MMAW, GMAW, oxy-fuel brazing and soldering) — Welding processes Code of Practice 2021 (Qld)
Oxy-fuel gas equipment and gas cylinder handling competency
Competency in the use of the flammable gas detector — how to bump test it, how to read percent LEL, and what to do when it alarms. A detector nobody can use is not a control.
Abrasive power tool competency, including disc selection, guarding and rpm rating

Crystalline silica awareness and training where masonry or concrete is cut or drilled — WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 529CD requires workers to be trained about the risks where the processing is high risk
Working at heights training; EWP operation — TLILIC0005 licence for a boom-type EWP of 11 m or more, EWPA card and site familiarisation under 11 m
Confined space entry to AS 2865 if any part of the work is inside a tank, pit or riser — that work needs its own SWMS
Respirator fit test under AS/NZS 1715, and clean shaven where a tight-fitting respirator is worn

Electrical work on the FIP field wiring, pump controllers or any energised installation only by a licensed electrical worker under the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld) and the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld)
First aid and CPR, and extinguisher use for the fire watch

steps.step: Plan the job, design the hot work out of it, and get the permit before you leave the yard
hazards: Hot work done when a cold method would have finished the job
No hot work permit, so the building's responsible person does not know a fire system is coming down
Asbestos in pipe lagging, gaskets, wall sheet or eaves where you will cut or drill
Flammable stock, LPG, solvents or combustible dust in the room that you find out about after the first spark
Permit written open-ended, so a long day runs on an expired permit with nobody watching the clock

controls.control: Have the pipe cut, threaded and grooved to length in the workshop and fabricate brackets on the bench. Nothing you finish at the yard has to be burnt into place on site.
Where a joint must be made on site, use grooved couplings, press-fit or threaded joints instead of welding, and cold-cut with a pipe cutter, bandsaw or recip saw instead of a grinder or oxy set.

Hot work permit raised and signed by the building's responsible person before any spark. The permit names the room, the plant, the start and finish times, the fire watch by name, and the 60 minute watch after the last spark. Maximum currency 8 hours (AS 1674.1). A new permit if the work stops for more than 2 hours or runs past the finish time on it.

Ask for the site asbestos register before cutting or drilling into any building fabric — lagging, gasket, wall sheet, ceiling — in any building built before 2004, or of unknown age. Asbestos-containing material was legally installed in Australia until 31 December 2003. A Queensland workplace in a building constructed after 31 December 1989 with no asbestos identified may lawfully have no register (WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 425(6)) — that means no register, not no asbestos. No register and a pre-2004 building means no cutting into building fabric until it has been identified. The register must be made readily accessible to you before you start, and given to you where the work risks exposure to airborne asbestos (s 427).

Ring the building manager the day before: confirm which systems come down, for how long, who signs the impairment, whether the building has sleeping occupants, and whether the site stores LPG, fuel, solvents, chlorinated degreasers or combustible dust anywhere near the work. If the answer to that last one is yes or unknown, the gas detector comes with you.

steps.step: Arrive, induct, and walk the work area with the permit issuer
hazards: Occupied building — you do not know the evacuation route, the warden or the assembly point
Combustibles within spark range, including what is behind and below you
Chlorinated solvents and degreasers in the area — UV off an arc turns the vapour into phosgene well beyond spark range
Voids, cable tray, gas lines and stock on the far side of the wall you are cutting near
Public, staff and other trades walking through the work area

controls.control: Hard barricade the work zone before anything else goes on the floor.
Sign in, take the site induction, and write down the evacuation signal, the assembly point and the warden's name on the front of the permit.

Walk the area with the permit issuer. Sweep 15 m in every direction — that is the hot work area under AS 1674.1, and it is not the 11 m (35 ft) figure used in the American standard — and physically look at the other side of every wall, the ceiling void above and the space below the cut. That is where hot work fires start.

Look for chlorinated solvents on the walk — trichloroethylene, perchloroethylene, brake cleaner, some degreasers. They do not have to be within spark range to hurt you: UV off an arc decomposes the vapour into phosgene at a distance. They come out of the whole area, not just out of the spark zone, and if they cannot be removed the work is not done with an arc.
HOT WORK IN PROGRESS signage at every entry to the zone. In a public area a spotter stands on the door.

Before touching anything, find and photograph the FIP (Ampac, Vigilant MX1, Pertronic F220, Notifier, Kentec), the ASE, the sprinkler main stop valve and the zone valve for your section, the pump controllers, the hydrant booster and the isolation register. Photograph the as-found panel screen and valve positions.
Boots, hi-vis and safety glasses on entering the plant room, before you start looking at valves.

steps.step: Isolate the fire system, book the monitoring off, and log it
hazards: The system that protects the building is now off — a fire in that hour has nothing to stop it
Unwanted alarm and a brigade turnout if the ASE is not isolated first
Detectors capped and forgotten, so the room stays blind after you leave
Sprinkler valve shut with nothing recorded, and left shut after the job
Somebody else operates the valve or recharges the section while you are cut into it

controls.control: Lock and tag the sprinkler stop valve shut with your own lock, your own tag and a strap or chain, so nobody can put water back into the section while you are cut into it. Leave the fire pump controllers in AUTO unless the work itself requires otherwise, and record it if you take them out.

Minimise the impairment. Zone or point isolate at the FIP rather than isolating the whole panel, and shut the floor or subsidiary sprinkler valve rather than the main stop valve where the system allows it. Be clear about what this is: the isolation is not a control — it is the hazard. The controls for it are in the next step and every one of them goes in before the first spark.

Book the ASE isolate with the QFD monitoring contractor (Johnson Controls, 1300 360 575) before you isolate, and write the isolation reference they give you on the permit. Confirm with the building's responsible person that the occupier's alternative protection arrangement for the isolation period is in place — QFD requires protection at least equivalent to the monitored system while the alarm is isolated. An ASE isolate longer than 12 hours needs Queensland Fire Department approval — arrange it beforehand, not at 4pm.
Sign the impairment onto the site isolation register or permit board with your name, your mobile, the time off and the time it must be back on.

Cap only the detectors in the room you are working in, use bright covers, write the number of caps on the job card, and photograph each cap as it goes on. You will count them back against those photos.
In a hospital, aged care, hotel or any building with sleeping occupants, do the work outside sleeping hours and get the occupier's written agreement to the isolation window before you isolate.

steps.responsible: Lead technician (QBCC fire protection licence holder)

steps.step: Put interim fire protection in place before the first spark
hazards: No detection and no suppression in the room you are about to set alight
Combustibles left within spark range, including under floor penetrations and inside cable tray
Sprinkler heads and detectors above the work operating from the heat of the work itself — usually on a different section from the one you isolated and drained
No one watching the work while the technician's helmet is down
Nothing at the work position to put a small fire out with, or the wrong extinguisher reached for next to energised gear

controls.control: Move the combustibles out — cardboard, pallets, chemicals, plastic pipe, ceiling tiles, waste bins — clear 15 m in every direction including behind and below. Chlorinated solvents and degreasers come out of the whole area, not just out of the 15 m: an arc turns the vapour into phosgene at a distance.
What cannot be moved gets covered with a fire or welding blanket. Seal floor penetrations, service holes, cable tray gaps and duct openings with a non-combustible cover — a rag is not a cover.

Look up before the first spark. Identify every sprinkler head and detector inside the heat plume of the work, not just the ones on the section you isolated — the ceiling protection above you is usually a different section, and a torch or a hot workpiece under a live head will trip it straight onto the FIP, the pump controller or the switchboard. Shield the head with a non-combustible cover, or isolate that section as well. Never hang a welding blanket so that it traps heat under a head.

Two 9 L water and one CO2 or 9 kg ABE extinguisher at the work position, not at the door — and know which one you are reaching for. Where the work is near the FIP, a pump controller or a switchboard, the CO2 is the first-attack unit: water and ABE powder do not go on energised gear or on the panel. Run out the hose reel where one is within reach and confirm it is charged. An extinguisher is response, not prevention — it does not make the work safer, it only limits what happens when the rest of this fails.
A dedicated fire watch with no other job. They stand where they can see the work and the far side of the wall, and they know where the nearest MCP is and the building's street address for 000.
The fire watch stays through the work and for 60 minutes after the last spark.

Where you cannot clear or inspect the full 15 m — an occupied floor, a tenancy you have no access to, a locked room on the far side of the wall — you do not proceed hot. Extend the barricade, put a second watch on the far side, or cold-cut.

steps.step: Set up the work position — access, height, and the exclusion zone below
hazards: Fall from an EWP, ladder or platform more than 2 m
Hot slag, sparks and offcuts falling onto people, stock or plant below
EWP struck by forklifts or delivery vehicles, or striking sprinkler pipe and services overhead
Poor footing on a wet, oily or cluttered plant room floor

controls.control: Prefabricate at ground level and lift the finished piece into place. Do the grinding on the bench, not overhead.
Work off a scissor lift, EWP or mobile scaffold with guardrails, mid-rail and toeboard intact. A ladder is access only — it is not a work platform for hot work.
Barricade the drop zone below with spark-proof screens or blankets hung over the edge. Nobody works or walks under the hot work while it is live.

EWP operator holds the ticket: TLILIC0005 for a boom-type EWP of 11 m or more, EWPA card and site familiarisation under 11 m. Pre-start recorded, and the floor checked for penetrations, pits and load rating before the machine goes on it.
Spotter on the ground wherever forklifts or vehicles move. Agree the traffic and exclusion plan with the site before the machine is set up.
In a boom-type EWP, full body harness and adjustable lanyard to AS/NZS 1891, clipped to the basket anchor point, never to the rail or to a service overhead.

steps.step: Prepare the pipe — drain it, prove it, test the air, and know what is in it
hazards: Cutting into a charged sprinkler or hydrant main — stored energy, pipe movement, and water into switchboards and the FIP
Cutting a line that has held fuel, gas, refrigerant or solvent
Flammable gas or vapour in the room or in the line — a hazardous atmosphere under WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 51(2)(c) once it exceeds 5% of the LEL, with a deliberate ignition source in your hand
Zinc fume from grinding or welding galvanised pipe
Asbestos gasket or lagging on old pipework
Weld slag, swarf and cutting burrs left inside the bore, which will disable the section with no fault showing at the panel

controls.control: Shut the section valve, open the drain and the test valve, and prove zero pressure on the gauge and at an open point before the blade goes in. Prove it — do not trust the valve.
Bucket, drip tray, plastic sheet and a wet vac under every cut. Know where the floor waste is. Cover the switchboard, FIP and pump controller before you open the pipe.

Where the site stores LPG, fuel, solvents or combustible dust, or where the pipe or vessel may hold vapour, gas-test before the first spark: test the hot work area and test inside the pipe, drum, tank or vessel you are cutting into, with a calibrated and bump-tested flammable gas detector, by someone competent in its use, no more than 2 hours before you start. The reading must be below 5% of the LEL. An atmosphere at or above 5% LEL is a hazardous atmosphere under WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 51(2)(c), and s 52 makes an ignition source in it something you must control — in plain terms, you do not strike an arc in it. Write the reading, the time and the tester's name on the permit.

Keep the detector running in the work area through the job, not just at the start. If it reaches 5% LEL at any point: stop, shut the gas at the cylinder, cancel the permit, ventilate, and do not restart until it reads clear again and a new permit is issued.
Confirm the line you are cutting is the line you isolated. Trace it end to end, tag both ends, and check it against the valve chart and the as-installed drawings.
Never hot-cut a line that has held anything but water or air. If it has held fuel, gas, refrigerant or solvent, stop and have it purged, cleaned and gas-tested by a competent person first.
On galvanised pipe, grind the zinc back at least 50 mm each side of the weld before striking an arc. Zinc fume gives you metal fume fever hours later.

Ream and deburr every cut before anything goes back together. Nothing is rejoined with swarf, slag or a burr in the bore — that debris ends up in a head or a nozzle and the panel will still read normal.

P2 minimum. P3 or powered air for galvanised, stainless, or a plant room with no ventilation. Fit-tested, clean shaven under the seal. Remember what it does not do: a particulate filter stops none of the ozone, nitrogen dioxide or carbon monoxide off an arc — that is what the extraction is for.

steps.step: Cutting and grinding
hazards: Sparks carrying up to 15 m, through gaps, down penetrations and into cable tray
Disc shatter, kickback and hot fragments to the eye
Noise above the exposure standard — WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 56 and 57, LAeq,8h 85 dB(A)
Respirable crystalline silica when drilling or cutting masonry and concrete for brackets
Burns from the hot workpiece and hot offcuts
Heat stress — plant room with no ventilation, sleeves down, leathers on, Queensland summer
Electric shock from leads and tools on a wet plant room floor

controls.control: Cold cut wherever the job allows — pipe cutter, bandsaw or recip saw. No sparks, no fire watch, no permit clock running.
Guard fitted, correct disc for the material, disc rated above the tool's rpm and inside its use-by date. No cut-off wheel used for grinding and no grinding wheel used for cutting.

Trap the sparks with a spark screen or fire blanket set on the run of the sparks. Where you are grinding on a concrete floor, wet the floor down first — but never where arc welding is in progress, and never where welding leads, extension leads or a return clamp are on the floor. If the floor is already wet and an arc has to go near it, dry the area first or cold-cut.

On-tool dust extraction, water suppression or local exhaust ventilation running whenever you drill or cut masonry or concrete. WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 529C says the processing of a crystalline silica substance must be controlled, and s 529B(1)(b) says controlled means at least one of wet suppression, on-tool extraction, local exhaust ventilation, an enclosed filtered cabin or isolating people from the dust is actually in use. Dry cutting or drilling masonry with no water and no extraction is not on, at any duration.
Every lead and tool through an RCD, kept off the floor and out of water.
Aim the sparks away from the work area and downward. That is technique, not a barrier — the screen is the barrier.
Leads tested and tagged before they leave the yard — AS/NZS 3012 for construction work, AS/NZS 3000 for the installation you are working near.

If the masonry work is more than incidental, that is an office call before the job, not a decision on the drill. Where the processing is high risk (WHS Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 529BA and 529CA), a written silica risk control plan is required before work starts (s 529CB) and must be complied with and reviewed (s 529CC), workers must be trained (s 529CD), and if air monitoring shows the exposure standard exceeded the results go to the regulator within 14 days (s 529CE). Ring the office — do not sort it out on the tool.

Work and rest cycles agreed before you start, water at the work position, and you and the fire watch check each other at every break — headache, cramps, no sweating, stumbling, confusion. On a hot day in an unventilated plant room, set up forced ventilation for the people, not just for the fume.
Face shield over safety glasses, Class 5 hearing protection, leather gloves, sleeves down. Nobody stands in the spark stream without the same PPE.

steps.step: Welding, brazing and soldering
hazards: Arc flash and arc eye to anyone in the room or walking past an open door
Welding fume — a Group 1 carcinogen; the workplace exposure standard for welding fumes (not otherwise classified) is 1 mg/m3 over eight hours

Cadmium fume from cadmium-bearing silver brazing alloy — delayed-onset chemical pneumonitis that has been fatal from a single short exposure, and it will feel like the metal fume fever this SWMS warns about elsewhere; fluoride flux fume; lead fume from old solder
Ozone, nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide off the arc — gases, which no particulate filter touches
Flashback or hose failure on an oxy-fuel set
Oxygen enrichment in a small plant room — clothing that would normally smoulder burns violently; acetylene decomposing explosively above 100 kPa with no oxygen needed
LPG or acetylene cylinder leak, fall-over or heating
Electric shock from the welder, wet floor, or a return path through building services
A live electrode holder or a live torch left unattended in an isolated building at smoko
Heat stress in full leathers and a respirator in an unventilated room

controls.control: Cadmium-free brazing filler only. Check the SDS before the rod goes in the bag — cadmium-bearing silver alloy does not come on a Safe QLD site. Lead-free solder on anything you are joining. Fluoride-bearing flux needs extraction, not just a P2.
Welding screens on every open side so nobody in the building catches an arc. Keep the plant room door closed or screened.

Fume extraction at the arc, or forced ventilation in the plant room. Keep your head out of the plume. In a small unventilated room extraction is not optional — no extraction and no ventilation means the arc does not get struck.
Flashback arresters to AS 4603 at both regulator outlets and non-return valves at the torch. Leak-test hoses with soapy water at start-up.
Cylinders upright and physically restrained — chained, strapped or in the trolley — so they cannot fall, and clear of the work and the walkway.
Welder on an RCD, with the work lead clamped directly to the piece. Never take the return through building steel, cable tray or the fire main — see AS 1674.2 and AS/NZS 3000.

Cylinder discipline: keys on the valves, cylinders stored and handled to AS 4332 and, for LP Gas, AS 1596. Cylinders never travel or sit in the cab or an unventilated van. A cylinder that has travelled lying down stands upright before it is used.

At every break and at the end of the day, on both sides of the kit. Gas side: shut off at the cylinder — not just at the torch — release the regulator adjusting screws, and pull the hoses out of any enclosed or confined space. Arc side: de-energise the welder at the supply, take the electrode out of the holder, and stow the holder where it cannot arc against anything. Nothing live gets left on the floor of an isolated building.

Never use oxygen to ventilate a room, cool yourself, blow down clothing or dust off the work. No oil or grease on oxygen fittings, regulators or gloves. Acetylene never above 100 kPa (15 psi) at the regulator — above that it can decompose on its own without any oxygen present.

Light blowpipes with a flint gun. No lighters, no matches, no rag or wick — a disposable lighter in the flame path is a burn to the hand, and a smouldering wick is exactly the ignition source this permit exists to stop.
Welders do not work alone. No fire watch on site means no hot work — you do not cover both jobs yourself and you do not weld in an empty plant room.
Where the gas test in the pipe preparation step applied, the detector is still running and still reading below 5% LEL before the arc is struck and while it is live.
Work and rest cycles, water at the work position, gear off in the rest break, and you and the fire watch check each other for heat illness every time you stop.
Correct shade filter to AS/NZS 1338.1, welding gloves, leather apron and spats, dry gloves and dry boots on a wet plant room floor.

steps.responsible: Welder or technician doing the hot work

steps.step: Fire watch during the work, and for 60 minutes after the last spark
hazards: A smoulder in a void, ceiling space, insulation or the far side of a wall showing itself 30 to 60 minutes after work stops
Hot slag sitting in cable tray, a penetration or a duct
The fire watch pulled off to hold a pipe or fetch a tool
No detection and no sprinklers to catch what the watch misses
Burns to the watch from hand-checking a surface that was at welding temperature

controls.control: The fire watch does nothing else. Not holding the pipe, not fetching tools, not on the phone.
Check the far side of every wall, the ceiling void above and the space below at the start, at every break, and at the end of the work.

Before the watch is stood down, run a thermal camera or an infrared thermometer over the work area and the far face of the wall. If you have neither on the truck, hold the back of your hand near the surface — near it, never on it — and if there is any doubt at all the watch keeps running.

The watch runs a full 60 minutes after the last spark. AS 1674.1 requires the area to be inspected after hot work to confirm nothing is left smouldering; it does not set the length of the watch for you. 30 minutes is the common insurer minimum. The Safe QLD rule is 60 because the fire system is off and there is nothing else watching the room. Do not close the permit and do not leave the building until that hour is done and logged.

If the watch sees smoke or fire: stop work, shut the gas at the cylinder, raise the alarm at the nearest MCP, ring 000, and only fight it if it is small and you have a clear way out behind you. Tell 000 the fire system is isolated.

steps.step: Put the fire system back on and prove it works
hazards: System left isolated overnight because the day ran late
Detector caps left on, so the room stays blind
Sprinkler stop valve left shut or part-open, and the valve monitor not checked
Weld slag, swarf and burrs left in the bore, which will block a head or a nozzle while the panel still reads normal
Monitoring left off, so the building looks protected but signals nowhere
One technician checking his own work, on exactly the failure modes a self-check does not catch
Unwanted alarm and brigade turnout when the system is restored

controls.control: Count the detector caps back in against the number on the job card and against the photo of each cap going on, then walk the room and look up. If the count is short, find it before you go anywhere.

Blow through or flush the section before you refill it, and confirm the flush runs clean at the drain or test valve. Slag, swarf and burrs left in the pipe end up in a head or a nozzle, and the panel will still read normal (AS 2118.1 for sprinkler, AS 2419.1 for hydrant).
Open the sprinkler stop valve fully, back it off a quarter turn, remove your lock and tag, and confirm the valve monitor switch shows no fault at the FIP.
De-isolate the FIP zones and points, clear every fault, and confirm the panel sits in normal — no isolates, no faults, no alarms. Photograph the screen.
Ring the monitoring contractor to lift the ASE isolate, confirm the signal path is back, and close out the isolation reference.

Prove the work. Alarm-test a device on the affected zone and confirm the correct zone and point reports at the FIP (AS 1670.1 and AS 1851-2012). Refill and pressurise the sprinkler section and check for leaks and correct standing pressure (AS 2118.1), or the hydrant section (AS 2419.1).

A second person witnesses and countersigns the restoration before the isolation is signed off — the cap count, the valve position, the panel-normal screen and the alarm test. A second technician if there is one on site, otherwise the building's responsible person, who can at least watch the cap count and the panel screen. If you truly cannot get a witness, write on the permit that the restoration was unwitnessed and tell the office before you leave site.
Sign the isolation off the register and tell the building's responsible person face to face that the system is back on.

steps.responsible: Lead technician (QBCC fire protection licence holder)

steps.step: Clean up, close the permit and report
hazards: Hot offcuts, discs and rods left where someone picks them up or bins them
Swarf and water left on the plant room floor, in a drain or under a switchboard
A defect found during the work left undocumented
Permit left open, so the site has no record the watch was completed

controls.control: A steel quench bucket of water at the work position from the start of the job. Every offcut, disc, rod and scoop of swarf goes straight into it, then into a lidded steel bin on the truck. Nothing hot goes into a plastic tub, a cardboard box or the site bin.
Bag it and take it away. Nothing you cut is left on site, hot or cold.
Clean the floor, clear the drip trays, and check no water sits in or under the switchboard, the FIP or a pump controller.
Close the hot work permit with the building's responsible person, with the fire watch finish time filled in, and leave them their copy.

Any defect you could not rectify goes on the job card and to the office the same day. AS 1851-2012 requires the responsible entity to be told of a critical defect before you leave site and confirmed in writing within 24 hours.
Attach photos of the finished work, the FIP in normal and the valve positions to the job before you drive away.

emergency:
FIRE: stop work, shut the gas off at the cylinder, raise the alarm at the nearest MCP, ring 000. Give the street address and the brigade entry point, and tell them the fire system is isolated and which part. Fight it only if it is small and you have a clear way out behind you. Do not assume the building will fight it for you — that is the point of the fire watch.

IF YOU DISCHARGE CO2 IN A SMALL PLANT ROOM: get out and ventilate before anyone goes back in. CO2 displaces the oxygen in a sealed room and you will not feel it coming.

BURN: cool under running water for 20 minutes. Do not peel clothing off a burn. Cover with cling film. Anything bigger than a 20c piece, or on the face, hands or a joint, goes to hospital.

ARC EYE: it comes on hours later. Rinse the eyes, cold compress, out of the light, see a doctor the same night.

FEELING FLU-LIKE HOURS AFTER HOT WORK: do not assume it is metal fume fever. If cadmium-bearing brazing filler or a fluoride-bearing flux was used, that is a hospital presentation the same day, not a lie-down — cadmium pneumonitis has a delayed onset and has been fatal. Tell the hospital exactly what you were brazing with and take the rod packet or the SDS with you. Metal fume fever from galvanised work still gets medical advice and still gets reported.

ELECTRIC SHOCK: do not touch the person. Kill the supply at the isolator or RCD, ring 000, start CPR if they are not breathing. They go to hospital even if they feel fine. Quarantine and tag out the tool and the lead.

FALL IN A HARNESS: get them down within minutes using the ground controls. Keep them moving their legs while you do it — suspension trauma kills faster than the fall did. Once they are down, lay them flat and keep them flat. Do not sit them up and do not hold them upright for 30 minutes, whatever an older SWMS says — ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.5 found no evidence for that practice and says it may be harmful. Ring 000; they go to hospital even if they say they are fine.

HEAT ILLNESS: stop, out of the heat, gear off, cool actively — water, wet cloths, air movement — and fluids if they are fully alert. Confusion, stumbling, collapse or hot dry skin with no sweating is an emergency: ring 000 and keep cooling while you wait.

GAS LEAK OR FLASHBACK: close the cylinder valve if it is safe to reach, clear and ventilate the area, do not relight until the kit has been checked.

FIRE SYSTEM STILL ISOLATED WHEN YOU HAVE TO LEAVE: it does not stay isolated overnight without the occupier knowing. Ring the building's responsible person and the office, hand over the fire watch in writing, and record it on the isolation register.

NOTIFIABLE INCIDENT (death, serious injury or illness, or a dangerous incident such as an uncontrolled fire or explosion): ring Workplace Health and Safety Queensland on 1300 362 128 immediately, do not disturb the scene, and tell the office. Notification is required under the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld).

activity: Flowing hydrants and the booster assembly at full bore, and running the electric and diesel fire pumps, for the AS 1851 routine and the Form 72.
