whenRequired:
Fill this in before any job where water is flowed at full bore or a fire pump is started: the six-monthly with a pump run, the annual hydrant flow test, and the five-yearly booster and pumpset test.

WHY THERE IS A SWMS AT ALL. Safe QLD has determined that this work is not testing of a minor nature. It involves full-bore flow, starting two independently powered fire pumps, work near energised pump controllers, work on or near a traffic corridor, and a fire system fully out of service while it is going on. Safe QLD therefore treats it as construction work under the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 289(2)(e) - 'the installation, testing or maintenance of an essential service in relation to a structure' - and prepares and complies with a SWMS regardless of how the exclusion at s 289(3)(d) ('testing, maintenance or repair work of a minor nature carried out in connection with a structure') is read. That is a company determination about how we work, not a settled point of law. Do not argue it at the kerb with anybody. Just work to the statement.

ON THE DAY, TICK WHICH HIGH-RISK CATEGORIES APPLY:
- s 291(f) confined space - where a below-ground booster chamber, valve pit or in-ground hydrant pit is opened. The wording is 'in OR NEAR', so opening one and working beside it counts, not only climbing in.
- s 291(j) chemical, fuel or refrigerant lines - where the work goes near the diesel day tank, its fuel lines or the fuel transfer pipework, which it does every time you check the day tank or hunt a leak.
- s 291(k) energised electrical - wherever there is a pump controller, which is every site with a pump.
- s 291(l) contaminated or flammable atmosphere - wherever there is a diesel pumpset.
- s 291(n) traffic corridor - where the booster is on a street frontage or the work is on or beside a road.
- s 291(o) powered mobile plant - where the booster is in a car park, loading dock or yard with forklifts or trucks.

BEFORE WORK STARTS. Fill in the version and date of this statement, Safe QLD Fire Protection as the PCBU, the site, the supervisor and their mobile, and the emergency fields, on the front of this statement. Then brief the crew through it and everyone signs on. The sign-on IS the consultation record - there is no separate form.

HOW THE CONTROLS ARE MONITORED AND REVIEWED. The supervisor named on the front checks during the job that the controls listed here are actually in place, not just written down, and asks the crew whether any of them is not working. Anything that changes - a control that will not work on this site, a hazard nobody listed, an incident, a near miss, a change of crew, a change of scope - stops the job. This statement is then reviewed and revised on the spot and everyone signs on again, as the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 302 requires. Where there is a principal contractor they get a copy before work starts (s 301). The signed copy stays on site and readily accessible while the work is on, and is kept afterwards as s 303 requires - and for at least 2 years if a notifiable incident happens in connection with the work.

WHAT THIS STATEMENT IS NOT. Going into a water storage tank, entering a below-ground booster chamber, or going onto a roof to a hydrant is a different statement - confined space or working at heights - not this one. Opening those pits and working beside them from the surface IS this one.
permits: Fire system impairment permit from the building manager, covering the hydrant system and both pumps. Filled in BEFORE you start, with all of it: the impairment start time; the maximum time the system may be impaired; the alternative protection or fire watch running for that whole period and who provides it; who can authorise an extension and their mobile number; and the standing instruction that on any real alarm the impairment is lifted immediately and the arriving fire crew is told at the booster exactly what is isolated. A permit with the fire watch line blank is not a permit - do not start.
Alarm signalling isolation booked with the monitoring company before you start, with a reference number, and logged at the FIP.
Road or footpath occupancy permit from the local council, with a traffic guidance scheme designed for the site and the posted speed, where cones, signs or devices go on a road or footpath.
Site permit to work and induction where the building or construction site requires one.
Hot work permit if a defect needs cutting, grinding or welding - that is a separate SWMS and it is not done in a room with a diesel day tank or gassing batteries.

Fire door hold-open record: where a pump room fire door is held open for ventilation during a run, record it on the impairment permit with the time it was opened and the time it was closed. Holding a fire door open defeats a prescribed fire safety installation in a building whose fire system is already impaired - it gets recorded like any other impairment.
ppe: High visibility garment to AS 4602.1:2024, class D/N for any dark, dawn or low-light work, worn any time you are outside the vehicle. Buy to the 2024 edition - AS 4602.1:2011 is superseded.
Safety boots, steel cap, non-slip sole - the ground will be wet.
Safety glasses to AS/NZS 1337.1:2010 as the minimum, on whenever a line is charged or a coupling is handled.

Goggles or a full face shield to AS/NZS 1337.1:2010 for two jobs specifically: taking a hand-held pitot reading at the jet, and breaking any coupling, cap or test point on a line that has been under pressure. Glasses alone are not enough for either.
Grip gloves for hose, coupling and booster cap work.
Class 5 earmuffs or plugs to AS/NZS 1270:2002, in your hand before you open the pump room door.
Waterproof jacket and wet weather gear for full-bore flow work.

Gas monitor on the collar in the diesel pump room: a carbon monoxide monitor as the minimum. Where the room has poor ventilation, or a long run is planned, use a monitor that also carries an NO2 sensor. Be clear about the limit of the standard four-gas monitor (O2, LEL, CO, H2S) - it has NO nitrogen dioxide sensor. If that is all you have, you are not monitoring NO2 and it is controlled only by running the ventilation and keeping your time in the room short. Say that out loud at the pre-start.

Gas monitor condition: calibration in date - check the sticker, not your memory - and bump tested on the day. A bump test proves the sensor and alarm respond; it is not a calibration and does not replace one.

Gas monitor alarm setpoints: a low alarm that alerts you and starts you leaving, and a high alarm to get you straight out, both set BELOW the workplace exposure limit for carbon monoxide, not at it. Confirm the current exposure limit when the monitor is calibrated and set the alarms from that - an alarm set at the exposure limit only tells you the limit has already been reached.

Sun protection for outdoor work at boosters, car parks and hardstands: broad-brim hat or a legionnaire flap under the hard hat, SPF 50+ sunscreen reapplied every two hours, UV-rated long sleeves, and tinted safety glasses in the open.
Hard hat where the site or the loading dock requires it.
Long sleeves down, no loose clothing, lanyards, rings or watches near a running pumpset.
training: QBCC fire protection occupational licence in the class QBCC publishes as 'Fire protection - water-based fire system - install and maintain - restricted to commercial and industrial types' (or the unrestricted 'water-based fire system - install and maintain'). That class covers installing and maintaining fire hydrant systems and fire hose reels, with or without pumps, and QBCC states that 'maintain' includes inspect and test of equipment. There is no separate current QBCC fire pumps class and no separate inspect-and-test class in the water-based stream - pumps and inspect-and-test sit inside the install-and-maintain class.

Know the limit on that licence: QBCC warns that fire protection licence class holders cannot personally perform or supervise regulated plumbing work without a licence for that work under the Plumbing and Drainage Act 2018 (Qld). Inspect and test work does not need one. The moment a defect means working on the pipework, stop and get someone who holds the plumbing licence.
Competent in the AS 1851-2012 Section 3 fire pumpset routines and Section 4 fire hydrant routines, and in completing Form 72.

Isolation and lockout: how to isolate a fire pump at its external isolator, isolate diesel start batteries, fit your own padlock and danger tag, and verify dead by attempting a start. Every technician on this work carries their own padlock and danger tags - one lock, one person, one key.

Audiometric testing, current, for every worker who enters a running pump room. Hearing protection is the only control we have for pump room noise, and that engages the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 58: audiometric testing within 3 months of the worker commencing the work, and at least every 2 years after that. Do not send a technician into a running diesel pump room who has not had it.

Traffic: whoever controls traffic holds current Queensland TMR traffic controller accreditation - in Queensland the unit of competency on its own is not authority to control traffic, the accreditation is. Whoever sets out the traffic guidance scheme holds the TMR accreditation for implementing one, and the scheme itself is designed by a TMR-accredited designer. Check the current unit codes and accreditation categories with TMR before you book anyone; the codes and the framework move, and an out-of-date ticket is no ticket.
HLTAID011 Provide first aid, current, with CPR.
Construction induction card (white card) where the site is a construction workplace.
Site induction, plus the building's own pump room induction where it has one.
Gas detector familiarity - reading the calibration sticker, bump testing, understanding what the monitor can and cannot detect, and knowing exactly what to do when it alarms.

steps.step: Plan the test at the desk before you drive out. Pull the last Form 72, get the system's pressure and supply numbers, and book the impairment in properly.
hazards: Turning up to a pumpset that cannot be safely run and starting it anyway
Boosting a system above its rated pressure because the number got invented at the kerb
Flowing into an occupied basement or car park nobody was told about
Emptying a fire tank mid-test and running the pump dry
Unwanted brigade turnout and the false alarm charge
A building left with no fire protection for longer than anyone agreed, with no fire watch
Sending a crew too small for the work, or one person to a diesel pump run
Thousands of litres of treated or rusty water into a drain that cannot take it

controls.control: If the last Form 72 or the site history shows no exhaust flue, a seized engine, missing coupling or fan guards, or a tank below its low-level mark, do not book the test at all. Raise the defect and quote the repair first. Do not send a crew to a job you already know they cannot safely do.

Where the booster is on a busy street frontage, book the test early morning or after hours rather than the middle of the day. If you do, book the lighting with it - task lights and lit or retroreflective signage go on the truck. Do not schedule dark work and turn up with a head torch.
Read the last Form 72 and the pump data plate: pump type, duty point, town main or tank supply, booster location, and how many pressure zones there are - one appliance test per zone.

Get the system's maximum working pressure and the booster pressure relief valve setting off the design documents, the block plan, the hydraulic schedule or the pump data plate, and write BOTH numbers and their source on the front of this SWMS before the day. That recorded figure is the boost pressure limit. It is not negotiable at the kerb and it is not the pump operator's opinion. No recorded figure means no boost test.

Work out and write down the expected reaction force at the test flow, from the flow rate and the outlet or nozzle size, and the anchor needed to take it. Whatever the number turns out to be, the standing rule does not change: no branch, diffuser or open outlet is held by hand at full bore, ever, by anyone.

Where the supply is a tank: get the tank capacity, the current level and the low-level mark, work out how long the planned flow can run before the tank hits a safe stop level, and write that STOP LEVEL and that run time on the SWMS. If the tank cannot support the test flow for the routine duration, the test plan changes before the day, not on site.

Fill in the impairment permit with the building manager before the day: start time, maximum impairment duration, the fire watch or alternative protection and who provides it, and who can authorise an extension with their mobile. If nobody at the building will provide a fire watch, the test does not go ahead - book it for a day when they will.
Book with the building manager at least 24 hours out. Confirm who holds the pump room key and the FIP key, and that they will be on site.
Book the alarm isolation with the monitoring company for the test window and get the reference number onto the job before you leave the office.
Where signs, cones or devices go on a road or footpath, get the council road occupancy permit and the traffic guidance scheme designed and sorted before the day, not at the kerb.

Find out where the discharge goes and confirm the receiving drain or pit can take that flow rate for that duration - a full-bore hydrant test puts thousands of litres through it. Find out whether the tank water is treated or dosed (chlorine, corrosion inhibitor, antifreeze) and whether there is any rust or sediment history, before it heads for stormwater. The general environmental duty under the Environmental Protection Act 1994 (Qld) s 319 applies to us on this job.

Set the crew before the day. Minimum two people for any full-bore flow, any booster test and any pump run. One person may do the desk work, the FIP isolation and the paperwork alone. Nobody runs a diesel fire pump alone, under any circumstances.

steps.step: On site, before anything is touched: fill in the front of this SWMS, brief the crew through it, and everyone signs on.
hazards: Crew working to a statement nobody has read
A control written here that does not exist on this site - no ventilation fan, no anchor point, no restraints, no isolator handle
Working alone or out of contact in a plant room with no phone coverage
The statement never being reviewed when the job changes underneath it
Emergency instructions pointing at an assembly area and a defib that nobody has identified

controls.control: STOP-WORK LIST. Any one of these and the job does not start, or stops where it is - no discussion, no working around it: no second person for a full-bore flow, booster test or pump run; no working mechanical ventilation in the diesel pump room; flue condition unknown or damaged; no gas monitor in calibration; no hose restraints on the truck; no fire watch for the impairment; no fixed anchor point for the diffuser or meter; no recorded maximum boost pressure. Raise the defect, ring the supervisor, come back with what is missing.

Fill in the front of this statement: version and date, PCBU (Safe QLD Fire Protection), site, supervisor and mobile, ASSEMBLY AREA, nearest first aid kit, nearest defibrillator, nearest hospital, and site contact and mobile. The emergency section of this SWMS points at those fields - if they are blank it points at nothing.

Walk the crew through this statement step by step. Ask them straight out what will not work on this site, and change it before you start rather than after. Everyone who will work to it signs on. The sign-on is the consultation record.

Confirm each control physically exists here before you rely on it - point at the ventilation fan, the anchor, the restraints, the isolator handle, the external engine stop, the drain. A control you cannot point at is a control that will not happen.

Communications: confirm phone or radio coverage at every work position, including inside the pump room, before anyone goes in. Where there is no coverage the standby person standing in sight and hearing IS the communication system - not the phone in your pocket.

Where one person is on site alone for the desk, FIP and paperwork part of the job, set the remote-work system the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 48 requires: a check-in interval, a named person in the office holding the check-in, and an agreed response when a check-in is missed - ring, then send someone, then ring 000.

Monitoring and review: the supervisor checks through the job that these controls are in place. Any change - a control that will not work, a new hazard, a near miss, a crew change - stops the job, this statement is revised on the spot, and everyone signs on again.

steps.step: Park up, walk the site, and set the work area where the booster is in a car park, loading dock, yard or private hardstand.
hazards: Cars, trucks and forklifts moving through the work area
Reversing the ute in a live car park
Public or staff walking into a charged line
Vehicle driving over a hose across a driveway
Working before daylight with no lighting
Sun and heat on an open hardstand or car park
Hose, cones, signs and gear blocking an exit, exit path or fire stair in a building whose fire system is about to be turned off

controls.control: Get the vehicle and the work off any trafficked route entirely - a closed bay, a blocked-off aisle, a hardstand corner. Do not work off the back of a ute sitting in a live aisle because it is closer to the booster.
Where movements cannot be stopped, move the work to a time when they are not happening - before the dock opens, after the shift, on the weekend.

Get the movements physically stopped, not just warned about: the dock roller door down, the aisle closed with barriers at both ends, the forklifts parked and keys out. Ring the loading dock or warehouse supervisor, get it done, and write down the name of who did it. It stays stopped the whole time the line is charged.
Where the hose has to cross a trafficked lane or driveway, use hose ramps or run it hard against the kerb. Never leave a loose line across a driveway.

Task lighting on stands, and lit or retroreflective signage, wherever the work is outside daylight hours. Light the booster, the hose run and the discharge point - not just where you happen to be standing. A charged hose across a path at 5am is invisible without it.
Cones and 'Fire Testing in Progress' signs delineate the work area. They warn people; they do not stop anything. Treat them as a warning and keep looking up regardless.
Reverse in on arrival so you drive out forward, and have the second person spot you out of the mirrors' blind spots.

Nothing - hose, cones, signs, cabinet doors, gear, the ute - blocks an exit door, exit path, fire stair or fire door at any time. Where a hose must cross an exit path it is ramped and attended. This matters more today than on any other day, because the building's fire system is out of service while you work.

Heat and sun: water in the vehicle and actually drink it, work in shade where there is any, swap the outside job with the second person on a hot day, and stop and cool down if anyone is cramping, headachy, confused or has stopped sweating.

High visibility garment to AS 4602.1:2024 on before you step out of the vehicle, and it stays on - class D/N for dark or low-light work. Sun protection on for outdoor work: hat or legionnaire flap, sunscreen, sleeves down.

steps.step: Set the work area where the booster is on a public road frontage, or the work is on or beside a live traffic lane.
hazards: Being struck by a vehicle - the thing on this job most likely to kill someone
A vehicle entering the work area at posted speed with only cones between it and the crew
Signs and tapers set at a distance guessed rather than derived from the posted speed
Public or pedestrians walking into a charged line or over a hose on a footpath
Brigade appliance manoeuvring at the kerb during the booster test
Working at a street booster before daylight

controls.control: Get off the road. Work from the footpath side, from inside the property boundary, or from behind a kerb build-out wherever the booster can be reached that way. Most street booster tests can be done without anyone standing in a traffic lane - plan it that way first, every time.
Where the road cannot be avoided, shift the work to the lowest-traffic window the impairment permit allows - early morning, after hours - and get the lane closed rather than shared.

Physical separation between live traffic and the crew: water-filled barriers, barrier boards, or a shadow vehicle, positioned as the traffic guidance scheme requires. Cones and signs are delineation - nothing about them physically stops a vehicle. If the scheme calls for physical separation and it is not there, the work does not start.
Hose ramps wherever a hose crosses a footpath or a lane, and task lighting plus lit or retroreflective signage for any work outside daylight hours.

Set signs and devices out at the advance warning and taper distances the traffic guidance scheme specifies for the posted speed at this site. Do not use a fixed distance out of your head - at 60 km/h the advance signs sit far further back than most people guess, and a short taper is worse than none. The scheme is designed by a TMR-accredited designer and set out by someone accredited to implement it.

A TMR-accredited traffic controller controls traffic wherever vehicles enter or cross the work area, including bringing a brigade appliance in and out for the booster test. That is their only job while they are doing it.
Keep your body out of the traffic space at all times, including while setting out and picking up. Face oncoming traffic. Never step backwards into a lane.
Nothing obstructs a footpath, exit path or fire stair. Where the hose crosses a footpath it is ramped and someone is watching it.
Heat and sun as for any outdoor work: water, shade, rotation, and stop if anyone shows heat symptoms.
Class D/N high visibility garment to AS 4602.1:2024 for everyone in or near the traffic space, day or night. Sun protection for outdoor work.

steps.responsible: Technician, second person and accredited traffic controller

steps.step: Open any in-ground hydrant pit, valve pit or below-ground booster chamber you need - and make it safe the moment it is open.
hazards: Heavy pit lid - back strain, crushed hands, crushed toes
Fingers under a lid as it drops back
The open hole itself as a fall, trip and step hazard, worse once the ground is wet
Snakes, spiders, wasps and vermin in a pit that has been shut for twelve months
A below-ground chamber that is a confined space
Standing water hiding the valve, the floor and the depth

controls.control: Do not enter a below-ground booster chamber or any pit you would have to climb into. If the valve or the connection can only be reached by getting in, stop - that is a confined space, and it needs a different statement, a different permit, atmospheric testing and a different crew. Test what you can reach from the surface and raise the rest as a defect.

The moment a lid is off, the hole is barricaded or covered - a pit guard, a board over it, or a person standing at it. Cones around an open pit on a footpath are not enough. Nobody walks away from an open pit, not for a minute, not to get a tool from the ute.

Use the proper lifting keys for the lid. Two people on any lid you cannot lift comfortably on your own, which is most fire pit lids. Lift with the legs, keep the lid between you, and slide it clear rather than carrying it.
Fingers and toes clear: hands on the keys only, boots back from the edge, and lower the lid under control - never drop it, never let it swing.
Before a hand goes in, look first with a torch and tap the lid to give anything living time to move. Never reach blind into a pit.
Where the pit is full of water so you cannot see the floor or the valve, pump or bail it until you can, or raise it as a defect. Do not feel around underwater for a valve.
Lids go back on properly, seated, before you leave that part of the site - and the barricades come in after the lid goes on, not before.
Gloves and boots for every lid. Safety glasses - grit and rust come off pit lids and out of pits.

steps.step: Isolate the brigade signal at the FIP, start the impairment clock, and get the fire watch on.
hazards: Brigade turnout on a pump start or flow switch, and the charge that follows
Occupants evacuating on the sirens
A real fire in a building whose hydrants and both pumps are out of service
The impairment quietly running past the agreed window
System left isolated overnight
Arriving fire crew not knowing what is isolated

controls.control: Impair no more than the test actually needs. Isolate only the inputs the test will trip, and only the zones you are working on. Never blanket-isolate the panel because it is quicker. Where the system can be tested a zone at a time and left protected everywhere else, do it that way even though it takes longer.
At the FIP, isolate the pump start and flow switch inputs to the alarm signalling equipment. Write the zone, the inputs isolated and the time in the FIP log book.

Where the impairment takes the water supply out - the five-yearly booster and pumpset test especially - the alternative protection agreed on the permit is in place BEFORE the isolation starts: a charged hose from an unaffected zone or an adjacent building, a standby appliance, or extinguishers and hose reels confirmed in service on every affected floor. Physically check it is there. Do not take it on trust.

The fire watch named on the permit starts before the isolation and stays until it is lifted: a person patrolling the affected areas with a means of raising the alarm and a phone. It is not the technician - you will have your hands full, your ears covered and your back to the building.

Write the impairment start time and the permit's maximum duration on the front of this SWMS and on the tag at the FIP. Set a phone alarm for 30 minutes BEFORE the window closes, not for the end of it, so there is time to restore rather than time to panic.
Ring the monitoring company, confirm the isolation is showing on their system, and write the reference number on the job before any water moves.
Tell the building manager and the chief warden what is isolated, that the sirens may sound, that the pump will run loud, how long for, and that the fire watch is on and who it is.
Hang your own isolation tag on the FIP door with your name, your mobile, the time isolated and the time it must be back on. Nobody else removes your tag.

Standing instruction, no exceptions: on any real alarm, or any sign of a real fire, the impairment is lifted immediately - pumps to auto, isolation off, monitoring rung - and the arriving crew is told at the booster exactly what is isolated and what is back in service.
Running past the window needs the person named on the permit to authorise it, by phone, with the new time written on the permit, on the FIP tag and on this SWMS. Nobody extends their own impairment.

steps.step: Pre-start the pump room before anything is started.
hazards: Diesel exhaust building up in an enclosed room - carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide
Flue disconnected, holed or discharging back into the room
Diesel or oil on the floor, leaking day tank, fuel lines weeping
Battery gassing hydrogen, acid on the terminals
Coupling or fan guard missing or loose
Heat exchanger cooling line shut or blocked, so the engine overheats during the run
Unguarded hot manifold and flue
Wet slippery floor you will be walking in ear muffs
Pump started with no water
Heat build-up in a small unventilated room

controls.control: If the exhaust flue is disconnected, holed, or you can smell exhaust in the room from a previous run, the diesel does not get started. Fail it on the Form 72 and raise the defect.

A pumpset with the coupling guard or fan guard off does not get started, and 'resting in place' is not on. Bolt it back on or fail it. Guarding of moving parts, and guarding or insulation of hot parts such as the manifold and flue, are duties on the person with management or control of the plant under the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) - so an unguarded coupling or a bare hot manifold within reach is a defect to write up, not a hazard for you to dodge all afternoon.

Stop-work: no working mechanical ventilation, no second person outside, no gas monitor in calibration, or a flue you cannot verify - the diesel does not run today. Raise the defect and come back with what is missing.

Run the room's mechanical ventilation and confirm it is actually moving air - hand at the grille, not just a lamp on a switch - before anything starts. Leave it running for the whole run and afterwards until the room is clear.

Where the door must be held open for extra ventilation, hold it with a person or a listed hold-open device - never a wedge, a brick or a fire extinguisher. A pump room door is normally a fire door: it is closed the moment the run ends, and the fact it was held open goes on the impairment permit.
Check the water supply before you touch a start button: tank level above the low-level mark, or the town main suction valve open and strapped.

Check the heat exchanger cooling water line is open, the strainer is clear, and water will actually reach it when the pump runs. An engine cooled off its own discharge with a shut cooling line will overheat within minutes of starting.
Check the fuel day tank level, and look at the floor, the bund and the fuel lines for diesel. Clean up a spill and find the leak before running anything.
Check battery electrolyte, terminals and that the charger is on float. No smoking, no naked flame, no grinder in this room.
Squeegee or mop a wet floor BEFORE the run, not after. You will be walking it later in ear muffs with your hands full and the engine going.
Class 5 hearing protection to AS/NZS 1270:2002 in your hand before you open the door, safety glasses on.

Gas monitor on your collar, calibration in date, bump tested this morning, low and high alarms set below the carbon monoxide exposure limit. It comes into the room with you every single time. Where the truck carries a second monitor, the standby person wears it at the door - one monitor between two people means the person outside is blind. If it has no NO2 sensor, say so out loud now: nitrogen dioxide is then controlled only by the ventilation running and by keeping your time in the room short.

steps.step: Lay out and connect the test hoses, restraints, diffuser and gauges.
hazards: Hose burst under full system pressure
Coupling not seated and blowing off when the line charges
Manual handling of 65 mm layflat hose
Using site occupant-use hose that is out of test date
No hose restraints on the truck, so couplings get charged bare

controls.control: Where a flow meter can be fitted on the test line, fit it and skip the hose and diffuser altogether. This is the single best control on this job - use it wherever the installation allows it, not just when it is convenient.
Use short company test hose rated above the maximum pressure at that outlet and in test date. Never grab the site's occupant-use hose off the rack for a flow test.

Hose restraints or safety straps fitted across every coupling on the line before it is charged. Restraints are standard kit on the vehicle, carried alongside the hose, and there are enough of them for every coupling in the run. No restraints on the truck, or not enough - the line does not get charged. Stop, raise it, come back with them.

Inspect every hose before it goes out - cuts, abrasion, weeping, lining condition, and the test date on the band. Any doubt and it does not get charged. Delivery layflat hose is serviced under AS 1851-2012 Section 8.
Check every Storz or instantaneous coupling is fully seated with the lug home, and pull-test the joint by hand before charging.
Run the hose out straight, no kinks, keep the run as short as the test allows, and keep it clear of exit paths, fire stairs and doorways.
Two people carry and lay the hose. Bend the knees, no twisting, take the couplings' weight.
Gloves and safety glasses on for all coupling work.

steps.step: Charge the line and flow the hydrant at full bore, taking flow meter or pitot and pressure readings.
hazards: Hose whip if a coupling lets go under pressure
Reaction force off an unrestrained diffuser or branch
Jet knocking a person off their feet, or high pressure water jet injection injury
Water hammer from closing the landing valve fast
Flooding into lift lobbies, switchrooms, basements
Hidden pit or open drain underfoot on wet ground
Aerosol off a main that has held stagnant water for twelve months - legionella in the breathing zone
Fire tank emptied and the pump run dry
Discoloured, chlorinated or inhibitor-dosed water into stormwater and into neighbours' taps

controls.control: Use the flow meter on the test line wherever the installation allows it and take the reading off the meter. Then nobody has to stand anywhere near the jet at all.
Nobody holds a branch, diffuser or open outlet by hand at full bore. Not for a second, not to steady it, not because it is nearly finished. Under any circumstances.
Everyone stands out of the line of the hose run while it charges, and behind the landing valve. Nobody stands over or beside a coupling as the line comes up to pressure.

Anchor the diffuser or flow meter outlet to a fixed structural point - a bollard, a post set in the ground, a structural rail. A strapped trolley, a wheelie bin, a parked ute or a mate's boot is not an anchor. If there is nothing on this site to anchor to, the flow does not go to full bore - raise it and get an anchor point installed.
Hose restraints fitted to every coupling on the charged line, checked again as the last thing before the valve is cracked.

Direct the discharge into the stormwater pit or grated drain confirmed at planning as able to take the flow. Not into a doorway, lift lobby, basement ramp, switchroom, or a car park bay with a vehicle in it. Not at a building air intake, an open window or an occupied doorway.
Open the landing valve slowly, a quarter turn at a time. Let the line fill and the air out before going to full bore, and close it just as slowly to stop water hammer.
One person on the landing valve, one at the diffuser, in sight of each other or on the radio, with an agreed hand signal for STOP that either can give. Nobody works alone on a charged line.

Taking the flow reading: off the flow meter, or off a pitot clamped or bracketed in the stream. Where a hand-held pitot is genuinely the only option, one nominated person holds it and does it this way - approach the jet from the side, never from in front; keep your torso, face and airway out of the jet line; brace the tube against your body and against the outlet so it cannot be snatched; hold it only as long as the gauge needs to settle; and take the reading at the lowest flow that still satisfies the routine. Everyone else stays clear. Nobody reaches across the stream.

Stand upwind of the discharge and keep the spray plume out of your breathing zone. A hydrant main that has sat still for twelve months is a recognised legionella reservoir, and full-bore flow through a diffuser makes a fine aerosol at head height that you will be standing in and soaked by. If the plume is blowing back over you, over a doorway, over a footpath or into an air intake, stop and reposition the discharge. Do not just wear it and get on with it.

Where the supply is a tank, one person watches the tank level for the whole flow and calls the STOP LEVEL agreed at planning. Shut down at that level, not when the low-level alarm goes, and not when the routine happens to finish.
Walk the discharge path first and note every pit, grate and step before the ground is wet, and make sure every pit you opened is barricaded or covered before the water goes on.
Tell the site, and the water authority, where a long full-bore draw off the town main is likely to discolour water to neighbouring properties.

If the water heading for the drain is treated, dosed, or visibly rusty or sedimented beyond ordinary discolouration: stop the flow, contain what you can, ring the building manager and the supervisor, and do not restart until the discharge point is sorted. Letting it run because the test has to be finished today is a breach of the general environmental duty under the Environmental Protection Act 1994 (Qld).
Safety glasses, gloves, boots and waterproof jacket. Goggles or a face shield for whoever holds a pitot at the jet. Hearing protection where the discharge is loud.

steps.step: Test the booster assembly, one connection per pressure zone, up to the maximum boost pressure recorded on the front of this SWMS.
hazards: Boosting above the system's rated pressure and splitting a riser inside an occupied building
High pressure at the booster inlets during the appliance boost
Blank cap or test point ejected off a pressurised inlet
Non-return valve failure back-pressurising the inlet side
Brigade appliance or test pump manoeuvring at the kerb
Traffic and pedestrians at a street frontage booster
Unrestrained booster hose at pressure
A gauge reading zero because it is blocked or isolated, not because the line is dead

controls.control: Depressurise before any spanner touches anything: bleed the assembly down, then OPEN THE BLEED OR DRAIN AND WATCH IT RUN DRY. Running dry is the proof the stored energy is gone. The gauge only confirms it - a gauge can be blocked, isolated or dead and will happily read zero on a live line.

Physically separate people from the pressurised assembly: barriers, or the vehicle positioned between the booster and any footpath or lane. Latch the cabinet doors open where they cannot swing into anyone and cannot block a footpath or an exit path.

Fit a test gauge rated well above the recorded maximum boost pressure. Confirm the assembly's pressure relief valve and non-return valves are in place and working before any boost - the relief valve is the only thing standing between an operator's throttle and a split riser.

The maximum boost pressure is the figure recorded on the front of this SWMS at planning, taken off the design documents, block plan, hydraulic schedule or pump data plate and checked against what is actually in front of you. It is not the appliance or test pump operator's opinion and it is not worked out at the kerb. No recorded figure, no boost test - go away and get the number.

Agree that figure and the hand signals with the appliance or test pump operator before a drop of water goes in, and confirm they can see you for the whole test. The operator raises pressure in stages on your signal, and drops it immediately on a stop signal from anyone.

Never crack a booster inlet cap or a test point while the assembly is pressurised. The person who bled it down is the person who says out loud that it is dead and ran dry, before anyone picks up a spanner.
Stand to the side of a pressurised inlet, never in front of it, and the same for anyone watching. Cones and signs warn the public, they do not stop them - keep looking up.
Test each booster connection separately where the system has more than one pressure zone, and record every one of them on the Form 72.
Where a brigade appliance is on site, the accredited traffic controller manages it in and out of the work area.
Safety glasses and gloves at the booster the entire time it is pressurised. Goggles or a face shield for breaking any cap, coupling or test point on a line that has been under pressure.

steps.step: Before any hand, tool or rag goes near either pumpset: isolate it, lock it, tag it, and prove it is dead.
hazards: Pump auto-starting on a pressure drop while hands are near the coupling, shaft or fan
A controller fault closing the contactor with the mode switch selected to OFF
Somebody else putting the pump back to auto while you are working on it
A diesel cranking off its start batteries with the controller off
The mains failure test on the electric pump starting the diesel with someone standing at it
415 V live inside the controller cubicle
Arc flash if the cubicle is opened

controls.control: Do not open the pump controller cubicle. Every AS 1851-2012 Section 3 test Safe QLD does is run from outside the cubicle - the start button, a pressure drop through the test line, and the external isolator handle. Anything that needs the cubicle open - failed contactor, burnt terminal, blown fuse - stops the job. Raise the defect and book a licensed electrician: electrical work in Queensland needs an electrical licence under the Electrical Safety Act 2002 (Qld), and work on or near energised electrical equipment is governed by the Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld).

ELECTRIC PUMP, hands-on work. Open the pump's external isolator - the same handle you already use for the mains failure test. Fit YOUR OWN padlock and danger tag to it. Then prove it: press start at the controller and confirm nothing happens and the controller is dead. Selecting OFF at the controller is a mode change, not an energy isolation - the incoming supply stays live behind it and a controller fault can still close the contactor. OFF is never the isolation.

DIESEL PUMP, hands-on work. All three, not one of them: controller to OFF; AND both start battery banks isolated, or the battery leads lifted, with your padlock and danger tag on the battery isolators; AND the manual start lever or handle secured so it cannot be operated. A diesel with battery power available will crank on a controller fault or a pressure drop no matter what the mode switch says. Then prove it: attempt a start and confirm it does not crank.

One lock, one person, one key. The person who fitted the lock is the only person who removes it. Nobody cuts or removes another technician's lock - ring them, and if you cannot reach them, ring the supervisor. The job waits.
Do the mains failure test by turning the external isolator handle only. Never pull a fuse, lift a cover or open a door to make the pump fail.

DUTY AND STANDBY - the thing this job catches people out with. On a set where the diesel backs up the electric pump, isolating or failing the electric pump is exactly what STARTS the diesel. The mains failure test WILL start the diesel. Before you touch that isolator: say it out loud, confirm everybody is clear of the diesel pumpset, and watch it start from well clear of its coupling, shaft and fan.

Between tests, when the pumps are back in auto and nothing is locked out, treat both as able to start at any moment. Hands, tools, rags and torches stay away from couplings, shafts and fans whenever a pump is in auto - there is no warning and no start-up delay.
Sleeves down, no loose clothing, no lanyard, no rings or watch anywhere near a pumpset. Hearing protection to hand.

steps.step: Run the electric fire pump - auto start on pressure drop, run up, and the mains failure test.
hazards: 415 V energised pump controller
Arc flash if the cubicle is opened
Pump auto-starting with no warning while hands are near the coupling
The mains failure test starting the diesel on a duty/standby set
Rotating shaft, coupling and motor fan
Casing overheating running at churn against a closed valve
Noise in a bare concrete pump room

controls.control: The cubicle stays shut. Start button, pressure drop through the test line, external isolator handle - that is the whole test, from outside. Anything else is an electrician's job and a separate visit.

Any hands-on work at the pumpset happens only under the lock-out in the previous step: isolator open, your own lock and danger tag on, start attempted and confirmed dead. Never on a mode switch selected to OFF.
Mains failure by the external isolator handle only. Never pull a fuse, lift a cover or open a door to make the pump fail.

Coupling and fan guards on and bolted for the whole run. A guard that has been removed goes back on before the pump is restarted - the regulation requires that plant cannot be restarted with the guarding off, so treat a missing guard as a hard stop.

Call 'STARTING THE PUMP' out loud before every start, and then actually look - at this pumpset and at the diesel that may start with it - to see nobody has a hand, a tool or a rag near a coupling, shaft or fan.
Do not hold it at churn against a closed valve any longer than the routine calls for. The casing heats fast. Open a flow path or shut it down.
Take the readings and get out. There is no reason to stand in a running pump room longer than the routine needs.
Hearing protection in before the pump starts, safety glasses on, sleeves down, no loose clothing, no lanyard hanging near the shaft.

steps.step: Run the diesel fire pump, with a standby person outside the door for the whole run, and take the run readings.
hazards: Carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide building up in an enclosed room
Noise well above the exposure standard in a bare concrete room
Burns off the exhaust manifold, the flue and the cooling system
Engine overheating on a shut or blocked cooling line, and a hot pressurised cooling system scalding on a cap or a hose
Rotating shaft and coupling
Diesel and oil, and hydrogen off gassing batteries
Heat build-up in a small unventilated room
A technician down inside, and a standby person whose instinct is to go in after them

controls.control: Stop-work: no working mechanical ventilation, no standby person outside, no gas monitor in calibration, or a flue you cannot verify - the diesel does not run. Raise the defect and come back. Nobody runs a diesel fire pump alone, on any site, for any reason.

The engine exhausts through a continuous flue direct to outside, and the room's mechanical ventilation runs for the whole run and afterwards until the room is clear. Those two things are what keep the air breathable. Everything else in this step is a check on them or a way of spending less time in there.

Coupling and fan guards on. Where a manifold or flue is unguarded and uninsulated within reach, raise it as a defect - the regulation puts a duty on the person with management or control of the plant to guard or insulate hot parts, so it is a defect to write up, not just a hot thing for you to remember not to touch.

Where the installation has remote or repeat gauges, or a camera on the gauge panel, use them and read from outside the room. Where it does not, and the routine is done here regularly, raise fitting them - that is the only real engineering fix for standing next to a running diesel to read a gauge.

Pre-start inspection before the engine turns over: flue continuous to outside, flexible section sound, no exhaust smell in the room, cooling water line open and strainer clear, guards on and bolted. Any one of those wrong and it does not start.

Take the readings from the doorway wherever the gauges and controller can be read from there. Where you have to go in, go in, take the reading, and come straight back out. You do not stand in the room for the run.
Keep the run to the duration AS 1851-2012 Section 3 requires and no longer. Longer is not better - it is just more exposure.

Watch the temperature gauge through the run and shut down on a rising trend - do not wait for the alarm. Touch nothing on the cooling system, including caps and hoses, until the engine has fully cooled. A hot pressurised cooling system will scald badly and it does not look hot.
Nothing goes near the manifold or the flue while it runs, or for 30 minutes after it stops.

STANDBY PERSON: stands outside the door where they can see you and hear the engine, with a phone or radio, for the whole run. That is their only job - not paperwork, not the truck. If you go down inside, THEY DO NOT ENTER. The emergency section of this statement sets out exactly what they do instead, and they read it before the engine starts. Settle one thing at the pre-start: if there is only one gas monitor and it goes in on the technician, the standby person does NOT go in at all - they stop the engine from outside, open up, ring 000 and wait at the door. Where you have a second monitor, the standby person wears it.
If the gas monitor alarms: out of the room, engine off, door open, ventilation running, and nobody goes back in until the monitor reads clear.
No hot work, no smoking and no grinding in a room with a diesel day tank and gassing batteries.

Class 5 earmuffs or plugs to AS/NZS 1270:2002 in BEFORE the engine turns over. The exposure standard is LAeq,8h of 85 dB(A) and LC,peak of 140 dB(C), and a diesel fire pump in a bare concrete room is well past it. Be straight about what that means: hearing protection is the ONLY control we have for that noise, so the hearing loss risk is carried, not removed. That is exactly why audiometric testing is required under the Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 58 - within 3 months of a worker commencing this work, and at least every 2 years after.
Gas monitor on the collar, calibration in date, bump tested today, low and high alarms set below the carbon monoxide exposure limit. Gloves and long sleeves against the manifold.

steps.step: Shut down, bleed the pressure off, drain, dry up and pack up.
hazards: Residual pressure still in the hose, the riser and the booster assembly
Hot engine, manifold, flue and pressurised cooling system
Slips on wet pump room and lobby floors
Manual handling of wet 65 mm hose
Water left sitting in a basement, lift pit or switchroom
Pit lids left off and barricades taken in too early
Pump room fire door left propped open

controls.control: Bleed every line and the booster assembly down, open the bleed or drain and WATCH IT RUN DRY, and confirm zero on the gauge, before a single coupling is broken. Running dry is the proof; the gauge is the confirmation. A blocked or isolated gauge reads zero on a live line.

Let the engine, the manifold, the flue and the cooling system cool before covers, caps, hoses or anything near them is touched. Thirty minutes minimum, longer on a hot day. Nothing about a hot cooling system looks hot.
Close the pump room fire door as soon as the run has ended and the room has cleared, and write on the impairment permit that it was held open and when it was closed.
Close the landing valve slowly, drain the riser at the low point, then check the drain valve is closed again.
Squeegee and mop water off the pump room floor, walkways and any lobby, and leave a wet floor sign out until it is dry. Do not leave it for the cleaner.
Drain and roll the hose with two people. Wet 65 mm hose is heavy - bend the knees, no twisting, share the lift, take the couplings' weight.
Lids back on every pit you opened, seated properly, and the barricades come in AFTER the lids go on, never before.
Walk the discharge path back and look for water in switchrooms, lift pits, plant rooms and car park bays. Photograph and report any damage the same day.
Gloves, and goggles or a face shield, for breaking any coupling on a line that has been under pressure. Boots stay on until the gear is on the truck.

steps.step: Restore the system, verify the restoration with a second pair of eyes, lift the impairment, and hand over.
hazards: System left isolated at the FIP overnight
Pump left in off or manual instead of auto
Suction or isolating valve left shut
Tank left below its low-level mark with the system back in auto
Booster cap or cabinet lock left off
A critical defect found today and never notified to the occupier
No record of the test or the defects
A building and its occupants with no fire protection and nobody aware of it

controls.control: Be clear-eyed about this step before you start it: every control here is a checklist, a phone call or a signature. There is no guard, no interlock and no engineering control that will catch a valve you left shut or a pump you left in manual. That is why the second-person verification below is not optional, and why this step is honestly rated medium residual and not low.

The job is not finished until every isolation is off and every valve is back to normal. It is the last thing done, before the cones come in, and nobody leaves site before it is done. If you are running out of time, you stay - you do not go home on an isolated system.

Remove your own padlocks and danger tags from the pump isolators and battery isolators yourself. Return both pumps to auto at the controller and confirm the auto lamp is actually lit on each one and no fault is showing.

Restoration checklist, item by item, out loud: every isolating and suction valve open and strapped or locked; tank level confirmed back above its low-level mark, or town main suction open and strapped; every booster cap on; booster cabinet locked; pump room fire door closed; both pumps in auto with the auto lamp lit; every drain valve closed; the FIP isolation removed; every pit lid on.

INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION. The second person walks the same checklist behind you, item by item, and signs it. Two sets of eyes on every restored item. Where you are genuinely alone, ring the supervisor and read the list to them and they countersign - a solo restoration is never self-verified.
Ring the monitoring company, get the de-isolation confirmed verbally against EACH input you isolated, and write the time and their reference in the FIP log book and on the job.
Take your tag off the FIP and photograph the panel showing normal, with no faults and no isolates. The photo goes on the Simpro job as the evidence that it was left right.
Write the impairment end time on the permit, stand the fire watch down and tell them personally, and tell the building manager and the chief warden that the system is back in service.

Where any defect found today is a critical defect, give the occupier a critical defect notice in the approved form within 24 hours after the maintenance. That is a statutory duty on the person who carried out the maintenance - us, not the office - under the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 53, and it is separate from the Form 72 and the Simpro job. Tell the building manager verbally before you leave as well. A tank left below its low-level mark with the system in auto is a critical defect.

Complete the Form 72 with every reading including each booster zone, sign it, record every defect, hand a copy to the building manager and file it on the Simpro job. The maintenance is carried out in compliance with QDC part MP 6.1, as the Building Fire Safety Regulation 2008 (Qld) s 50 requires of the person doing it.

This SWMS, signed on by everyone who worked to it, goes on the Simpro job. It stays available while the work is on and is kept afterwards - and for at least 2 years if a notifiable incident happened in connection with the work.

steps.responsible: Technician, verified and countersigned by the second person or the supervisor

emergency:
ASSEMBLY AREA, NEAREST FIRST AID KIT, DEFIBRILLATOR, NEAREST HOSPITAL AND SITE CONTACT are filled in on the front of this SWMS at the pre-start brief. If those fields are blank the brief is not finished - fill them in before you start work, because everything below points at them.

DIESEL PUMP ROOM - GAS ALARM, OR ANYONE FEELING UNWELL: hit the engine stop and get out. Door open, ventilation running. Do not go back in until the room has aired out and the monitor reads clear. Anyone who comes out of a room with the diesel running and has a headache, nausea, confusion, dizziness, or has just gone quiet, is treated as carbon monoxide exposure - fresh air, sit them down, ring 000 and say carbon monoxide. Do not let them drive themselves anywhere.

STANDBY PERSON - TECHNICIAN COLLAPSED INSIDE THE PUMP ROOM. YOU DO NOT ENTER. Not to drag them out. Not for a second. Not while holding your breath. Going in is how one casualty becomes two, and it is the most common way people die in exactly this situation. What you do, in this order:
1. Stop the engine from OUTSIDE - the external stop or the external isolator. Do not step into the room to reach a stop button.
2. Open the room right up - door and any external vents - and get the ventilation running.
3. Ring 000. Say carbon monoxide. Say there is a person down inside a plant room. Give the address, the pump room location, and how to get in.
4. Stay at the door. Keep everyone else out - including site staff who will want to help. Rescue from a carbon monoxide atmosphere is done by trained rescuers wearing breathing apparatus. That is not you and it is not the building manager.
5. Ring the Safe QLD supervisor.
6. Do not go back in at all unless you have a gas monitor of your own in your hand, it reads clear in the doorway, and the room has thoroughly aired with the ventilation running. The crew usually carries ONE monitor and it went in on the technician's collar - so on most jobs the honest answer is that you do not go in, you wait at the door for the fire crew. If you do go in with a monitor reading clear, get them out to fresh air and start CPR and the defibrillator.

BURST HOSE OR A COUPLING LETTING GO: shut the landing valve or the booster supply first, from behind and out of the line of the hose. Never chase a whipping line to grab it.

WATER JET OR HIGH PRESSURE INJECTION INJURY: 000 and hospital, even where the entry mark looks like nothing at all. Tell the hospital it was a high pressure water injection - it matters to how they treat it.

ELECTRIC SHOCK AT THE PUMP CONTROLLER OR SWITCHBOARD: do not touch the person, and do not touch anything they are in contact with. Isolate the supply - but only if you can reach the switch without entering the fault zone and without touching the person or what they are touching. If you cannot reach it safely, ring 000 and wait; do not improvise with a broom handle or a dry rope. Once they are clear of the supply: 000, CPR, defibrillator. Anyone who has taken a shock goes to hospital for assessment even if they get straight up and say they are fine - the dangerous heart rhythm can come hours later. An electric shock is a notifiable incident.

FLOODING INTO A SWITCHROOM, LIFT PIT OR BASEMENT: shut the flow off at the landing valve, ring the building manager straight away, and get the affected electrical supply isolated by the site's electrician before anyone walks in.

STRUCK BY A VEHICLE AT THE BOOSTER: 000, do not move them, and the traffic controller closes the road.

REAL ALARM OR REAL FIRE WHILE YOU ARE TESTING: the building has no working fire system and that is our doing, so getting the information to the brigade matters more than the paperwork. If you are already standing at the FIP and it takes seconds - pumps to auto, isolation off, go. If you are not at the panel, or it will take longer than seconds, leave it and go. Either way, get to the warden and to the arriving fire crew, at the assembly area or the booster, and tell them plainly: what is isolated, what state both pumps are in, which zones are affected, and where the fire watch is. Do not stay at a panel during a fire and do not go back to one.

NOTIFIABLE INCIDENT - death, serious injury or illness, or a dangerous incident such as an uncontrolled high pressure release, an electric shock, an escape of a substance, or an uncontrolled fire: ring Workplace Health and Safety Queensland on 1300 362 128 straight away, do not disturb the scene beyond what is needed to help someone or make it safe, and tell the Safe QLD supervisor. The site is preserved until an inspector says otherwise.

siteSpecificPrompts: FRONT OF STATEMENT - fill in before the brief: SWMS version and date. PCBU: Safe QLD Fire Protection. Site and address. Supervisor name and mobile. Then every worker signs on below after the brief.

EMERGENCY FIELDS - fill in before the brief: ASSEMBLY AREA. Nearest first aid kit. Nearest defibrillator. Nearest hospital and how long to it. Site contact name and mobile. Site evacuation signal. The emergency section points at these - if they are blank it points at nothing.

Maximum working pressure of this system, and the booster pressure relief valve setting. Where did each number come from - design documents, block plan, hydraulic schedule or pump data plate? Write the source. No source means no boost test.

Expected reaction force at the test flow, and the FIXED STRUCTURAL anchor you will use for the diffuser or flow meter. Name the actual anchor - 'we'll find something' is not an answer, and a trolley is not an anchor.

Water supply - town main or tank? If tank: capacity, level now, low-level mark, and the STOP LEVEL you will shut down at. Who watches the level during the flow, and how long can the flow run before it hits that level?
Impairment: start time, maximum duration off the permit, who provides the fire watch and their mobile, who can authorise an extension and their mobile.

Where is the pump room, who holds the key, and is the diesel exhaust flued all the way to outside? Note the flue condition before you start. Does the room have mechanical ventilation, and does it actually run?
Is the pump room door a fire door? Who or what holds it open during the run, and who closes it after? Record it on the impairment permit.
Where is the external engine stop for the diesel, reachable from outside the room? If there is not one, the standby person needs to know that before the engine starts.
Where is the external isolator for each pump, and where are the diesel start battery isolators and the manual start lever? Do you have your own padlock and danger tags on the truck?
Is the diesel the standby to the electric pump? If yes, everybody on site must know before the mains failure test that it WILL start the diesel.
Where is the booster - street frontage, car park, or loading dock? How many pressure zones and therefore how many appliance tests?

What traffic runs past the booster: public road, car park, forklifts? What is the posted speed? Who designed the traffic guidance scheme, who sets it out, and who is the accredited traffic controller? If the answer is a car park, who stops the forklifts and trucks, and what is their name?
Is any of this work outside daylight hours? If so, what lighting is on the truck and where does it go - booster, hose run, discharge point?

Where does the discharge go? Name the pit or drain, say what is downhill or downstream of it, confirm it can take the flow rate for the planned duration, and note the wind direction and any air intake, open window or occupied doorway near it.
Is the tank water treated or dosed - chlorine, corrosion inhibitor, antifreeze? Any rust or sediment history? What is the plan if it cannot go to stormwater?

Any in-ground pits or below-ground chambers to be opened? How heavy are the lids, do you have the right lifting keys, and how will you barricade them once open? Is any of them a confined space - if yes, stop, it is a different statement.
Which exits, exit paths, fire stairs or fire doors does the hose run, the cones or the work area come near? How will they be kept clear and who is watching them?
Which monitoring company, and what is today's alarm isolation reference number?
Is there phone or radio coverage in the pump room? If not, where does the standby person stand, and what is the agreed hand signal for STOP and for HELP?
Minimum crew for today, and who is the standby person for the diesel run? If it is only you, the diesel does not run.
Gas monitor serial number, calibration due date, and today's bump test result. Does it carry an NO2 sensor - yes or no? What are the low and high alarm setpoints?
Is audiometric testing current for everyone who will enter the running pump room today? Date of last test for each.

title: Testing a fire detection and alarm system in an occupied building
activity: AS 1851-2012 Section 6 routine service and functional test of a fire detection and alarm system while the building is occupied — isolating the fire indicator panel (FIP) and alarm signalling equipment (ASE) to the fire monitoring centre, locking off any gaseous, pre-action or deluge release, testing detectors and manual call points, running sounders and strobes at full volume, proving ancillary interfaces to lifts, air handling, smoke control, shutters and door holders, then restoring the system to normal and proving it back.
